entries.text: Shikaakwa, near enough, for the wild leek that grows thick along its banks in spring. The smell of it hangs over the marsh in April. The French wrote it down as Chicagou and the Americans dropped the end. Chandonnai, the trader's clerk, can say it the old way and the French way and the American way. Ask him to say all three.

levels.8-10: We call it Shikaakwa, or close to that. It is named for the wild leeks that grow thick on its banks in spring. In April the marsh smells of them. The French wrote it down as Chicagou, and the Americans dropped the end. Chandonnai, the trader's helper, can say it the old way, the French way and the American way. Ask him to say all three.

entries.text: For a village, no: too wet, too many mosquitoes, the ground floods every spring. For a crossing, the best on the lakes. Every canoe from the north going down to the Illinois comes through here and over the portage. Whoever sits at this river mouth hears everything first.

levels.8-10: For a village, no. It is too wet, there are too many mosquitoes, and the ground floods every spring. But as a crossing, it is the best on the lakes. Every canoe from the north going down to the Illinois River comes through here and over the carrying path. Whoever sits at this river mouth hears all the news first.

entries.text: Traded from the Sauk, who had it from somebody on the Missouri, who had it from somebody further west. A horse walks a long way before it reaches you. I gave four good beaver packs and a gun for him, and I have never regretted it.

levels.8-10: I traded for him with the Sauk. They got him from someone on the Missouri River, who got him from someone farther west. A horse walks a long way before it gets to you. I gave four good bundles of beaver furs and a gun for him. I have never been sorry.

entries.text: Most, but not all. There are Ottawa from the north, and Ojibwe, and a few Winnebago and Kickapoo who came to see what would happen. We three, Potawatomi, Ottawa and Ojibwe, call ourselves brothers: the three fires. We came down the lakes together long ago, and we still speak nearly the same language.

levels.8-10: Most are, but not all. There are Ottawa from the north, and Ojibwe. A few Winnebago and Kickapoo came to see what would happen. We three, the Potawatomi, Ottawa and Ojibwe, call ourselves brothers. We are the three fires. Long ago we came down the lakes together. We still speak almost the same language.

entries.text: Brothers never agree. The Ojibwe in the far north barely see an American from one year to the next. The Ottawa trade with the British at Mackinac. We Potawatomi live next to the Americans. We have the most to gain and the most to lose.

levels.8-10: Brothers never agree. The Ojibwe live far to the north. They hardly see an American from one year to the next. The Ottawa trade with the British at Mackinac. We Potawatomi live right next to the Americans. We have the most to win and the most to lose.

entries.text: They are angry and they are not our relatives, and when something bad happens, people say: the Winnebago did it. Sometimes it is true. It is very convenient for everybody else when it is.

levels.8-10: They are angry, and they are not our kin. When something bad happens, people say the Winnebago did it. Sometimes that is true. It is very handy for the rest of us when it is.

entries.text: From the traders, mostly the British ones at Mackinac and Malden, and from the Americans here when they were selling. Every autumn a man needs powder, lead, flints and a gun that works. Without them his family does not eat in winter. A gun is a hoe for meat.

levels.8-10: From the traders, mostly the British ones at Mackinac and Malden. We got them from the Americans here too, when they were selling. Every fall a man needs powder, bullets, flints and a gun that works. Without them his family has no meat in winter. A gun is a tool for getting food, like a hoe.

entries.text: The British give presents every year: guns, blankets, kettles, silver, tobacco. They call it keeping the friendship bright. The Americans give presents too, but fewer, and they want land at the end of it. A man notices which friend asks for nothing back.

levels.8-10: Every year the British give presents. They give guns, blankets, kettles, silver and tobacco. They say it keeps the friendship bright. The Americans give presents too, but fewer. And at the end, they want land. A man notices which friend asks for nothing back.

entries.text: After tomorrow, yes. Whatever happens tomorrow, my wife wants the corn in, and the corn does not care about the Americans.

levels.8-10: After tomorrow, yes. My wife wants the corn in, no matter what. The corn does not care about the Americans.

entries.text: Enough to trade and enough to swear. My mother's sister married a Frenchman at St. Joseph, so I grew up with French cousins who ate their corn on a plate and crossed themselves before thunder. Half the people at this river have a French grandfather somewhere.

levels.8-10: Enough to trade, and enough to say bad words. My mother's sister married a Frenchman at St. Joseph. So I grew up with French cousins. They ate their corn on a plate. They made the sign of the cross when it thundered. Half the people at this river have a French grandpa somewhere.

entries.text: My uncle and I, two summers ago. Birch bark from the north, sewn with spruce root, sealed with pitch, over cedar ribs. A bark canoe weighs no more than a man can carry on his shoulders, which is why we can cross the portage with it and the French can, and the Americans with their heavy boats cannot.

levels.8-10: My uncle and I made it, two summers ago. We used birch bark from the north and sewed it with spruce roots. We sealed it with tree sap, over a frame of cedar. A bark canoe is light enough for one man to carry on his shoulders. That is why we can carry it from one river to the next, and so can the French. The Americans, with their heavy boats, cannot.

entries.text: Shawneeawkee, we call him, the silversmith, because he worked silver when he first came among us, and still makes brooches for our women. He has lived at this river longer than the fort. He knows every family and what every family owes him, to the muskrat.

levels.8-10: We call him Shawneeawkee, the silversmith. When he first came among us, he made things out of silver. He still makes pins for our women. He has lived at this river longer than the fort has. He knows every family. He knows what every family owes him, down to the last muskrat skin.
levels.11-13: We call him Shawneeawkee, the silversmith. He worked silver when he first came among us, and he still makes pins for our women. He has lived at this river longer than the fort has stood. He knows every family, and what every family owes him, down to the last muskrat.

entries.text: Many do. Archange, across the river, is married to the Frenchman Ouilmette, and her father was a Frenchman too, and her mother one of us. A trader with a Potawatomi wife has a hundred relatives in the camps who will trade with him and nobody else. That is good for him. A Potawatomi woman with a trader husband has kettles and cloth and a house with a floor. That is good for her.

levels.8-10: Many do. Archange lives across the river. She is married to the Frenchman Ouilmette. Her own father was a Frenchman too, and her mother was one of us. A trader with a Potawatomi wife has a hundred relatives in the camps. They will trade with him and nobody else. That is good for him. A Potawatomi woman with a trader husband has kettles, cloth, and a house with a floor. That is good for her.

entries.text: We are neighbours, which means we sometimes do and sometimes do not. The Potawatomi came south into country that was once ours. We have married each other's daughters for a hundred years. We have also stolen each other's horses for a hundred years. Both things are true at once.

levels.8-10: We are neighbors. So sometimes we do, and sometimes we do not. The Potawatomi came south into land that was once ours. For a hundred years we have married each other's daughters. For a hundred years we have also stolen each other's horses. Both things are true at once.

entries.text: At the Fallen Timbers, eighteen summers ago, when I was very young, against General Wayne's soldiers. The Americans won. The nations made the treaty at Greenville. Since then the Miami have kept the peace, as Little Turtle said we should.

levels.8-10: Yes. It was at Fallen Timbers, eighteen summers ago. I was very young. We fought General Wayne's men, and the Americans won. Then the tribes made a treaty at Greenville. Since then the Miami have kept the peace, as Little Turtle said we should.

entries.text: For the officers' families, in the kitchen and the wash-house and the garden, from before light until after dark. Cooking, carrying, scrubbing, minding the children. The work does not stop because the army is leaving. If anything it doubles.

levels.8-10: I work for the officers' families. I work in the kitchen, the wash house and the garden, from before sunrise until after dark. I cook, carry, scrub and mind the children. The work does not stop because the army is leaving. If anything, there is twice as much.

entries.text: That is Captain Wells, the captain's wife's uncle, come up from Fort Wayne with about thirty Miami to bring us out. He rode through the gate yesterday afternoon on a fine horse, and every man on the walls cheered. He knows this country and these people better than anybody alive.

levels.8-10: That is Captain Wells. He is the uncle of the captain's wife. He came up from Fort Wayne with about thirty Miami to lead us out. He rode through the gate yesterday afternoon on a fine horse. Every man on the walls cheered. He knows this land and these people better than anyone alive.

entries.text: Tecumseh, if you want a name. The Shawnee who has been riding from nation to nation for years, telling every people from the lakes to the gulf to stand together against the Americans. His brother the Prophet has the visions. Tecumseh has the plan. He has gone over to the British now.

levels.8-10: Tecumseh, if you want a name. He is a Shawnee. For years he has ridden from nation to nation. He tells every people from the lakes to the gulf to stand together against the Americans. His brother, the Prophet, has the dreams. Tecumseh has the plan. Now he has joined the British.

entries.text: Ensign Ronan? He came to us straight from the military academy at West Point, and he is as straight as a ramrod and about as bendable. He thinks the captain is too timid. He says so, which young officers are not supposed to do.

levels.8-10: Ensign Ronan? He came to us straight from the army's school at West Point. He stands as straight as a ramrod, and he bends about as much. He thinks the captain is too timid. He says so out loud. Young officers are not supposed to do that.

entries.text: A Potawatomi man named Winnemeg carried it from General Hull at Detroit, through the woods, alone, with the letter sewn into his clothes. He came in on the ninth. Five days ago. Every day since, the camps round us have filled up a little more.

levels.8-10: A Potawatomi man named Winnemeg brought it from General Hull at Detroit. He came through the woods alone. The letter was sewn into his clothes. He got here on the ninth. That was five days ago. Each day since then, the camps around us have filled up a bit more.

entries.text: When the officers are not looking, which is most of the time. Cards, dice, a game with knucklebones that a Canadian taught us. We play for tobacco and buttons and a promise of tomorrow's whiskey ration, which nobody will get now.

levels.8-10: When the officers are not looking, which is most of the time. We play cards and dice. We play a game with little bones that a Canadian taught us. We bet tobacco, buttons, and the whiskey we were to get tomorrow. Now nobody will get it.

entries.text: There is a private from Kentucky who never loses. He says he was raised by a riverboat gambler. He owes nobody anything and everybody owes him something. Tonight he forgave every debt in the barracks. Nobody said why. Nobody needed to.

levels.8-10: There is a man from Kentucky who never loses. He says a riverboat gambler raised him. He owes no one, and everyone owes him. Tonight he let every man off what he owed. Nobody said why. Nobody had to.

entries.text: County Tyrone, by way of Philadelphia, by way of a recruiting sergeant and a pint of rum. I signed for five years and I have done four of them, and I have seen more of America from inside a blue coat than most Americans ever will.

levels.8-10: County Tyrone, in Ireland. Then Philadelphia. Then a sergeant who signed me up with a cup of rum. I signed up for five years, and I have done four of them. I have seen more of America in a blue army coat than most Americans ever will.
levels.11-13: County Tyrone, in Ireland, then Philadelphia, then a recruiting sergeant and a cup of rum. I signed up for five years and I have served four of them. I have seen more of America from inside a blue coat than most Americans ever will.

entries.text: Some of the old chiefs meant it, I am certain. Black Partridge meant it. Whether they can make their young men keep it is another thing. A chief among the Potawatomi leads by persuasion, not command. And persuasion has been going the other way all summer.

levels.8-10: Some of the old chiefs meant it, I am sure. Black Partridge meant it. But can they make their young men keep the promise? That is another thing. A Potawatomi chief leads by talking people into things. He cannot give orders. And all summer the talking has gone the other way.

entries.text: They were not from the villages close by, as far as anybody could tell. Winnebago, people said, though nobody knows for sure. But after that night, every visitor at the gate was a stranger until he proved otherwise. That is a terrible way to live beside your neighbours.

levels.8-10: They were not from the villages close by, as far as we could tell. People said they were Winnebago, but no one knows for sure. After that night, every man at the gate was a stranger until he showed he was not. That is a hard way to live next to your neighbors.

entries.text: On the north bank of the river, across from the fort, where the Kinzies and the Ouilmettes and a few more families have their houses. We cross by canoe. There is no bridge, and the river is deep enough to drown a careless man.

levels.8-10: On the north bank of the river, across from the fort. The Kinzies, the Ouilmettes and a few more families have their houses there. We cross by canoe. There is no bridge. The river is deep enough to drown a careless man.

entries.text: Crowded. We have been inside the walls since April, mostly, sleeping in the barracks or in the officers' houses, cooking for our families over somebody else's fire. Mrs. Heald and Mrs. Helm keep us organised. Without them I think we would have murdered each other by June.

levels.8-10: Crowded. We have mostly lived inside the walls since April. We sleep in the barracks or the officers' houses. We cook for our families over somebody else's fire. Mrs. Heald and Mrs. Helm keep us in order. Without them, I think we would have been at each other's throats by June.

entries.text: She is a Kentucky girl, Captain Wells's niece, and she rides a horse better than her husband does. She married him at twenty and came here on horseback through the woods with her servant Cicely. She has a temper, but she is fair, and she has never once looked down on any of us.

levels.8-10: She is a girl from Kentucky. Captain Wells is her uncle. She rides a horse better than her husband does. She married him at twenty and came here on horseback through the woods, with Cicely, the woman who works for her. She has a temper, but she is fair. She has never once looked down on any of us.

entries.text: I am an engagé, a hired man, for Mr. Kinzie. I paddle his canoes, carry his packs over the portage to the Des Plaines, and take his trade goods to the winter camps on the Illinois and the Rock River. Ninety pounds on my back and a song in my mouth, that is how we go.

levels.8-10: I am a hired man for Mr. Kinzie. I paddle his canoes. I carry his bundles over the path to the Des Plaines River. I take his goods to the winter camps on the Illinois and Rock rivers. Ninety pounds on my back and a song in my mouth. That is how we go.

entries.text: The path from the South Branch of this river, across a little marsh, to the Des Plaines, which runs down to the Illinois and the Mississippi. In spring when the water is high you can paddle almost the whole way. In August you drag the canoe through mud up to your knees and the mosquitoes eat you alive.

levels.8-10: It is the path from this river to the Des Plaines River. It goes from the South Branch, across a little marsh. The Des Plaines runs down to the Illinois River, and then to the Mississippi. In spring the water is high, so you can paddle most of the way. In August you drag the canoe through mud up to your knees. The bugs eat you alive.

entries.text: The greatest war leader the Miami ever had. Twenty-one years ago he beat General St. Clair's army on the Wabash, the worst defeat the Americans ever had from our people. Then he saw that we could not keep winning, and he made peace at Greenville, and he kept it until he died, this July, at Fort Wayne.

levels.8-10: He was the greatest war leader the Miami ever had. Twenty-one years ago he beat General St. Clair's army on the Wabash River. It was the worst loss the Americans ever had against our people. Then he saw that we could not keep winning. So he made peace at Greenville. He kept that peace until he died, this July, at Fort Wayne.

entries.text: Because the captain has promised goods to everyone, and because word came that the soldiers are leaving. There are people here from the villages on the Fox, the Kankakee, the Calumet, the Des Plaines, the Milwaukee. Some came for the blankets. Some came for other reasons.

levels.8-10: The captain has said he will give goods to everyone. And we heard the soldiers are leaving. People came from the villages on many rivers. They came from the Fox, the Kankakee, the Calumet, the Des Plaines and the Milwaukee. Some came for the blankets. Some came for other reasons.

entries.text: The soldiers poured the whiskey into the river and the powder down the well. They promised and then took back. The young men have been listening to Tecumseh's messengers all summer, and to Main Poc's. Mackinac has fallen. Detroit is next. A young man who wants to be a warrior will not have a better chance than tomorrow.

levels.8-10: The soldiers poured the whiskey into the river and the powder down the well. They promised, and then they took it back. All summer the young men have listened to messengers from Tecumseh and Main Poc. The British have taken Mackinac. Detroit is next. A young man who wants to be a warrior will not get a better chance than tomorrow.

entries.text: Furs. Muskrat, beaver, otter, mink, raccoon, deer hides. We bring them to the trader Kinzie and he gives us cloth, kettles, knives, guns, powder, silver, blankets. In a good winter a family can trap enough to buy everything it needs for a year.

levels.8-10: Furs. We trade muskrat, beaver, otter, mink, raccoon and deer skins. We bring them to Kinzie the trader. He gives us cloth, kettles, knives, guns, powder, silver and blankets. In a good winter, a family can trap enough to buy all it needs for a year.

entries.text: Deer in the oak groves along the river, all year. Ducks and geese by the thousand in spring and autumn, on the marshes west of here. Fish in the lake and the rivers: sturgeon, whitefish, pike. In the winter, our men go far out on the prairie for the elk and buffalo, though there are fewer buffalo every year.

levels.8-10: Deer live in the oak woods by the river all year. In spring and fall there are ducks and geese by the thousand on the marshes west of here. There are fish in the lake and the rivers, like sturgeon, whitefish and pike. In winter our men go far out on the prairie for elk and buffalo. But there are fewer buffalo every year.

entries.text: He is the greatest speaker I have ever heard. Two summers ago he came to a council on the Fox River and talked for a whole afternoon, and nobody moved. He said the land belongs to all the nations together, and no one nation can sell it. He said the Americans will not stop until they reach the western sea.

levels.8-10: He is the greatest speaker I have ever heard. Two summers ago he came to a meeting on the Fox River. He talked for a whole afternoon, and nobody moved. He said the land belongs to all the nations together. No one nation can sell it. He said the Americans will not stop until they reach the ocean in the west.

entries.text: I look at the treaties. Every few years, another treaty, another piece of land, another promise. My father's village was on land the Americans now call theirs. Tecumseh did not invent that. He only said it out loud.

levels.8-10: I look at the treaties. Every few years there is a new one. Each time, there is more land lost and one more promise. My father's village was on land the Americans now call theirs. Tecumseh did not make that up. He only said it out loud.

entries.text: It is a silver medal with the face of the American President on it, given at a treaty to a man the Americans want to treat as a chief. To the Americans it means: this man is our friend and speaks for his people. To us it means: this man made a promise, and wears it on his chest.

levels.8-10: It is a silver medal with the American President's face on it. The Americans give it at a treaty to a man they want to treat as a chief. To the Americans it means, "This man is our friend, and he speaks for his people." To us it means, "This man made a promise, and he wears it on his chest."

entries.text: In summer we live in long houses of bark and mats over bent saplings, by the river, near the cornfields. In winter we break into small family camps in the woods and live in round lodges covered with cattail mats, warm and dark, with the fire in the middle and the smoke going out at the top.

levels.8-10: In summer we live in long houses by the river, near the cornfields. They are made of bark and mats over bent young trees. In winter we split into small family camps in the woods. We live in round lodges covered with cattail mats. They are warm and dark. The fire is in the middle, and the smoke goes out the top.
levels.11-13: In summer we live in long houses of bark and mats over bent young trees, by the river, near the cornfields. In winter we split into small family camps in the woods. We live in round lodges covered with cattail mats, warm and dark, with the fire in the middle and the smoke going out the top.

entries.text: Go down to the camps by the river, but go with someone known. Archange Ouilmette, whose husband is the Frenchman across the river, has relations in every lodge here. Go with her, and they will give you food. Go alone, tonight, and nobody can tell you what will happen.

levels.8-10: Go down to the camps by the river, but go with someone people know. Archange Ouilmette is married to the Frenchman across the river. She has family in every lodge here. Go with her, and they will give you food. If you go alone, tonight, nobody can say what will happen.

entries.text: You ask me that straight to my face? You are bold. I will tell you this: I have been told by my elders to keep the peace and by Tecumseh's messengers to take back our country, and I have been told by the soldiers that they would give us whiskey and powder, and then they threw them in the river.

levels.8-10: You ask me that to my face? You are bold. I will tell you this much. My elders told me to keep the peace. Tecumseh's messengers told me to take back our land. The soldiers told us they would give us whiskey and powder. Then they threw them in the river.

entries.text: Sugar time, in the spring, when the snow is still on the ground and the maple sap is running. The whole village goes to the sugar bush and the women boil sap day and night in big kettles over fires, and the children run around with sticky hands and nobody sleeps much.

levels.8-10: Sugar time, in the spring. The snow is still on the ground, and the maple sap is running. The whole village goes to the maple woods. The women boil sap day and night in big kettles over fires. The kids run around with sticky hands. Nobody sleeps much.
levels.11-13: Sugar time, in the spring, when the snow is still on the ground and the maple sap is running. The whole village goes to the maple woods. The women boil sap day and night in big kettles over fires, and the children run around with sticky hands, and nobody sleeps much.

entries.text: The end of winter, before sugar, when the dried corn is running out and the hunting is poor and the children are thin. That is when you learn who your relatives are. Everybody shares or everybody starves.

levels.8-10: The end of winter, before sugar time. The dried corn is running out. The hunting is poor. The children are thin. That is when you learn who your family is. Everybody shares, or everybody starves.

entries.text: Every child is named by an elder who has dreamed the name, a few days after the birth. The name comes from the spirits, so it is not to be joked about. A man may get another name later, for something he does, and use that instead.

levels.8-10: An elder names every child a few days after it is born. The elder has dreamed the name. The name comes from the spirits, so nobody jokes about it. Later a man may get another name for something he does. Then he may use that one instead.

entries.text: They used to. They ran races along the beach and threw sticks into the lake for the dogs and argued in a language made of everybody's words. My son learned to say no in English before he could say it properly in ours.

levels.8-10: They used to. They ran races on the beach. They threw sticks into the lake for the dogs. They argued in a language made of everybody's words. My son learned to say "no" in English before he could say it right in ours.

entries.text: I remember the treaty at Greenville, seventeen summers ago. All the nations of the Northwest went to General Wayne's camp in Ohio, after his soldiers beat us at the Fallen Timbers. We sat for weeks. In the end we gave up most of Ohio and a few small pieces here and there, including six miles square at the mouth of this river.

levels.8-10: I remember the treaty at Greenville, seventeen summers ago. General Wayne's soldiers had beaten us at Fallen Timbers. Then all the nations of the Northwest went to his camp in Ohio. We sat there for weeks. In the end we gave up most of Ohio and a few small pieces of land here and there. One of them was a square of land six miles wide at the mouth of this river.

entries.text: Not as long as the Miami, who were here when the French came. My grandfather's people came south from the St. Joseph and the lakes, eighty or a hundred summers ago. The Miami moved east. Now the Potawatomi have the country from the Milwaukee to the Kankakee.

levels.8-10: Not as long as the Miami. They were here when the French came. My grandpa's people came south from the St. Joseph River and the lakes. That was about a hundred summers ago. The Miami moved east. Now the land from the Milwaukee River to the Kankakee is ours.

entries.text: Two blockhouses with cannon on top, the barracks for the soldiers, the officers' houses, the magazine where the powder was (they threw it down the well!), the store, the bakehouse, and the flagpole. There are two walls of logs all the way round, with sharp points on top.

levels.8-10: There are two blockhouses with cannons on top. There are barracks for the soldiers and houses for the officers. There is the powder room, where the powder was. They threw it down the well! There is the store, the bakehouse and the flagpole. Two log walls go all the way around, with sharp points on top.
levels.11-13: There are two blockhouses with cannons on top. There are barracks for the soldiers, the officers' houses, and the powder room where the powder was kept. (They threw it down the well!) There is the store, the bakehouse and the flagpole. Two walls of logs go all the way around, with sharp points on top.

entries.text: The hoop game: you roll a hoop of willow and throw a stick through it while it rolls. And lacrosse, with sticks with nets, which the big boys play so hard that someone always gets hurt. And the moccasin game, where you hide a stone under one of four moccasins and the other side guesses. The men gamble on it all night.

levels.8-10: The hoop game. You roll a willow hoop and throw a stick through it while it rolls. And lacrosse, with sticks that have nets. The big boys play so hard that someone always gets hurt. And the moccasin game. You hide a stone under one of four moccasins, and the other side guesses. The men bet on it all night.

entries.text: Because a stranger who hears it might remember it later, when people ask what Black Partridge did. Somebody should remember the truth.

levels.8-10: A stranger who hears it may tell it later, when people ask what Black Partridge did. Somebody should know the truth.
levels.11-13: Because a stranger who hears it may remember it later, when people ask what Black Partridge did. Somebody should remember the truth.

entries.text: At the lake the French call Peoria, on the Illinois River, many days south of here. My village is there, and my fields. I came up the Illinois and the Des Plaines for the council and for the goods, and because Kinzie and I are old friends and I wanted to see him before whatever comes.

levels.8-10: At the lake the French call Peoria, on the Illinois River. It is many days south of here. My village is there, and my fields. I came up the rivers for the meeting and for the goods. I also came because Kinzie and I are old friends. I wanted to see him before whatever comes.

entries.text: The Americans in the south are building more cabins every year, and their militia go riding through our country looking for horse thieves. A people can only be called horse thieves so many times before some of them decide to steal horses. My village has been quiet. That is my doing, and it is getting harder.

levels.8-10: The Americans in the south build more cabins every year. Their soldiers ride through our land looking for horse thieves. You can only call people horse thieves so many times before some of them decide to steal horses. My village has stayed quiet. I made it so, and it is getting harder.

entries.text: To stay with the wagons, keep together, and not fire unless fired on. Twelve of us, farmers and boatmen and a cooper, with muskets from the store. Griffith there was one of us until he signed on as a regular in April. He knows our company and the regulars both.

levels.8-10: To stay with the wagons, keep together, and not shoot unless someone shoots at us. There are twelve of us. We are farmers, boatmen and a barrel maker, with guns from the store. Griffith over there was one of us, until he joined the real army in April. He knows our group and the real soldiers both.

entries.text: Potawatomi from my mother, French from my father, English from the trader's books, Ottawa and Ojibwe because they are almost the same, and enough Miami and Winnebago to buy a horse. Six, if you count the language of a man who owes you money, which is universal.

levels.8-10: I speak Potawatomi from my mom and French from my dad. I speak English from the trader's books. I speak Ottawa and Ojibwe, because they are almost the same. And I know enough Miami and Winnebago to buy a horse. That makes six. Or seven, if you count the language of a man who owes you money. Everybody speaks that one.

entries.text: That the trader's family has fed his people for years and owes them nothing and is owed a great deal. That if the Kinzies are harmed, the traders will not come back to this river for a generation. That a careful man thinks about next winter as well as tomorrow. Go and ask him if he was listening. He was.

levels.8-10: I told him this. The trader's family has fed his people for years. They owe them nothing, and they are owed a lot. If the Kinzies are hurt, the traders will not come back to this river for a long, long time. A careful man thinks about next winter, not just tomorrow. Go and ask him if he was listening. He was.

entries.text: In Kentucky, at the Wells place near Louisville, in the kitchen, from the time I was a girl. Then Miss Rebekah married the captain and I was part of what she brought with her, like the linen and the silver. We came north on horseback through the woods. I carried my baby the whole way on my hip.

levels.8-10: In Kentucky, at the Wells place near Louisville. I worked in the kitchen from the time I was a girl. Then Miss Rebekah married the captain. I was part of what she brought with her, like the sheets and the silver. We came north on horseback through the woods. I carried my baby on my hip the whole way.

entries.text: Because she has heard the stories of women carried off to the camps and never seen again, and because she is the kind of woman who says a thing once and means it forever. I married her for that. Tonight I wish she were a little less certain about everything.

levels.8-10: She has heard stories of women taken to the camps and never seen again. And she is the kind of woman who says a thing once and means it forever. I married her for that. Tonight I wish she were a little less sure about everything.

entries.text: It is what the chief said, when he came to me this summer: the linden birds have been singing in my ears. I did not understand until the interpreter told me. He meant he had heard something he could not say aloud, and he was telling me without telling me. A man can warn you in a way that he can deny later.

levels.8-10: It is what the chief said when he came to me this summer. He said, "The linden birds have been singing in my ears." I did not understand until the man who knew his language told me. The chief had heard something he could not say out loud. He was telling me without telling me. A man can warn you in a way he can say he never did.

entries.text: Form the men, hold the ground, protect the wagons, and make a bargain if a bargain can be made. That is all an officer can do with fifty-four regulars, twelve militia, and a column of families on a beach between sand hills and the lake. Wells and his Miami will ride ahead and tell me what is coming.

levels.8-10: Line up the men, hold our ground, protect the wagons, and make a deal if a deal can be made. That is all an officer can do. I have fifty-four soldiers, twelve men from the town, and a line of families on a beach between sand hills and the lake. Wells and his Miami will ride ahead and tell me what is coming.

entries.text: He is the most stubborn, gentle, frightening man I have ever known. When I was a girl in Kentucky he used to tell me stories about the Miami villages and his wife Sweet Breeze, and then stop in the middle and go out and walk around the yard by himself. I did not understand then that he was homesick for a place he had chosen to leave.

levels.8-10: He is the most stubborn, gentle and scary man I have ever known. When I was a girl in Kentucky, he told me stories about the Miami villages and his wife, Sweet Breeze. Then he would stop in the middle and go walk around the yard by himself. I did not understand then. He was homesick for a place he had chosen to leave.

entries.text: I am Mrs. Kinzie's daughter by her first husband, so the trader is my stepfather, and Johnny and the little ones are my brothers and sisters. I grew up at Detroit and came here as a girl. I learned Potawatomi from the women who came to sell corn and French from the engagés. My English is the best of the three, my mother says, which is a pity because it is the least useful here.

levels.8-10: My mom is Mrs. Kinzie, and the trader is my stepdad. Johnny and the little ones are my brothers and sisters. I grew up at Detroit and came here as a girl. I learned Potawatomi from the women who came to sell corn. I learned French from the hired men. My mom says my English is the best of the three. That is too bad, because it is the least useful here.

entries.text: Years ago, when he came west as governor, before he was a general against us. A tall, quiet man who wrote everything down. He asked about my village and my family and my hunting grounds, and he wrote that down too. I did not know then that a man who writes down your hunting grounds is counting land.

levels.8-10: Yes, years ago, when he came west as governor, before he was a general fighting us. He was a tall, quiet man who wrote everything down. He asked about my village, my family and my hunting grounds. He wrote that down too. I did not know then that a man who writes down your hunting grounds is counting land.

entries.text: Josette will tell them stories in Ottawa and French until they fall asleep, and I will give the baby sugar on a rag, and John will sit in the stern and look as if nothing is the matter. Children believe a calm face more than any words. I learned that among the Seneca. When I was small and frightened, the women there would just keep working and humming, and after a while I stopped crying.

levels.8-10: Josette will tell them stories in Ottawa and French until they fall asleep. I will give the baby sugar on a cloth. John will sit at the back of the boat and look as if nothing is wrong. Children believe a calm face more than any words. I learned that among the Seneca. When I was small and scared, the women there just kept working and humming. After a while I stopped crying.

entries.text: Shawneeawkee. I came to this country as a boy apprentice to a silversmith in Quebec, and I ran off from that, but the trade stayed in my hands. When I first came among the Potawatomi I made brooches and ear bobs and arm bands, and they named me for it. I still make a brooch now and then, for a wife or a daughter in the camps.

levels.8-10: They call me Shawneeawkee. I came to this land as a boy who was learning to make silver things in Quebec. I ran away from that, but the skill stayed in my hands. When I first came among the Potawatomi, I made pins, earrings and arm bands. They named me for it. I still make a pin now and then, for a wife or a daughter in the camps.

entries.text: Because it was there when I bought it. A Frenchman named Le Mai had it, and before him Point de Sable, the man from Saint-Domingue, the first who ever really lived here. I bought the house and its poplars and its bake oven in 1804, the same year the soldiers came to build the fort across the water.

levels.8-10: Because it was there when I bought it. A Frenchman named Le Mai owned it. Before him, it belonged to Point de Sable, the man from Saint-Domingue. He was the first person who ever really lived here. I bought the house, its poplar trees and its bread oven in 1804. That was the same year the soldiers came to build the fort across the water.

entries.text: My mother's people knew Mrs. Kinzie, and when she needed someone to mind the children who could speak to them the way the children of this river speak, they sent me. I am the girl in the house who is half French and half Ottawa and wholly in charge of the little ones.

levels.8-10: My mother's people knew Mrs. Kinzie. She needed someone to care for the children who could talk to them the way kids talk at this river. So they sent me. I am the girl in the house who is half French and half Ottawa, and all in charge of the little ones.

entries.text: Some of the officers' wives came walking through my corn in the spring, before the trouble, laughing, pulling the young ears to look at them. I told them in my own language what I thought. One of them asked the interpreter what I had said. He told them something polite.

levels.8-10: Some of the officers' wives came walking through my corn in the spring, before the trouble. They laughed and pulled off the young ears to look at them. I told them in my language what I thought. One of them asked the man who knew both languages what I had said. He told them something polite.

entries.text: The Americans at Fort Wayne gave out whiskey to buy land. The Americans in Indiana hanged two of my relatives for killing a man who had stolen their horses. The Americans here poured our whiskey into the river last night after promising it to us. Pick any one of those. I have more.

levels.8-10: The Americans at Fort Wayne gave out whiskey to get land. The Americans in Indiana hanged two of my family. Those men had killed a man who stole their horses. The Americans here poured our whiskey in the river last night. They had said it was ours. Pick any one of those. I have more.

entries.text: Corn, squash, beans, tobacco, a few rows of potatoes, and some French things my mother would recognise: sorrel, chives, a pear tree I grew from a pip I carried from Montreal in my pocket. It has borne pears for three years. This year they will be ripe in September, and I intend to be here to eat them.

levels.8-10: Corn, squash, beans, tobacco, and a few rows of potatoes. There are some French plants my mother would know, like sorrel and chives. There is a pear tree I grew from a seed I carried from Montreal in my pocket. It has grown pears for three years. This year they will be ripe in September. I plan to be here to eat them.

entries.text: Count the lodges. My mother's people are Potawatomi and they married into every village from here to the Kankakee. When I walk through the camps, every other woman calls me sister or aunt or daughter. That is why my husband thinks we are safe. He is right, I think, mostly.

entries.text: Mathematics, engineering, gunnery, French, and how to stand very straight while being shouted at. There are not many of us yet, maybe a hundred officers in the whole army who went there. We are supposed to be the new kind of officer: educated, professional, not some politician's nephew.

levels.8-10: Math, building forts and bridges, firing cannons, French, and how to stand very straight while being yelled at. There are not many of us yet. entries.text: East of here, round the bottom of the lake, on the St. Joseph River, where the French had a fort and a mission long ago. My people have lived there for many lifetimes. It is good country: rich bottoms, sugar maples, sturgeon in the river in spring.

levels.8-10: East of here, around the bottom of the lake, on the St. Joseph River. The French had a fort and a church there long ago. My people have lived there for many lifetimes. It is good land. There is rich soil by the river, maple trees for sugar, and sturgeon in the river in spring.

entries.text: Calomel, jalap, laudanum, quinine bark, some lint and bandages, a set of instruments I bought in New York, and a little book of remedies. It is not much against what may come. I spent the afternoon cutting bandages from a bolt of the factory's linen, and I have rolled them all and put them where I can reach them.

levels.8-10: Medicines for fevers, for the stomach and for pain. Some cloth and bandages. A set of tools I bought in New York, and a little book of cures. It is not much against what may come. levels.8-10: The haystacks at Lee's Place in 1812. They stand across the river from the cabin. The owner said they looked like smooth, pale domes. So they were made again. Now they are lumpy, as if piled up by hand. Bits of hay stick out. Hay is stamped flat at the bottom. Each stack has its own shape. Some are fresh. Some have sunk down. Cows have eaten from some, and some have been cut.
levels.11-13: The haystacks at Lee's Place in 1812, on the bank across from the cabin. The owner said they looked like smooth, pale domes, so they were made again. levels.14-15: The haystacks at Lee's Place in 1812, on the bank across from the cabin. They were rebuilt after the owner reported that they looked like smooth, pale domes. entries.card: notes:Built by Jean Baptiste Point du Sable, 'a native of San Domingo and a negro', an Indian trader who lived in it for over eighteen years (Currey). John Kinzie's family home and the base of his trade from 1804, 'the family mansion of my husband' in Wau-Bun.
entries.text: Built by Jean Baptiste Point du Sable, 'a native of San Domingo and a negro', an Indian trader who lived in it for over eighteen years (Currey). John Kinzie's family home and the base of his trade from 1804, 'the family mansion of my husband' in Wau-Bun.

levels.8-10: Jean Baptiste Point du Sable built this house. Currey says he came from San Domingo and was a Black man. He traded with the Native people and lived here for over eighteen years. From 1804 it was John Kinzie's family home and the center of his trade. Wau-Bun calls it "the family mansion of my husband."

entries.card: notes:Currey 1912 ch. II, Gutenberg #52346 plain text lines 1360-1369: 'The Indians continued to come and go on their nomadic excursions according to their habit, and while in this vicinity they lived in their wigwams near the river, their favorite camping place being at a point on the south bank near the present State Street bridge. A swale or gully opened into the river there, reaching back as far as the present line of Randolph Street. The movements of the Indians were regarded with great interest by the traders located in the neighborhood, who were anxious to sell them supplies in exchange for the furs brought in by them'. That families came and went to trade all year, and camped by the river near the creek's mouth while here, is Currey's; that some lodges stood there on any day is inferred from it.
entries.text: Currey 1912 ch. II, Gutenberg #52346 plain text lines 1360-1369: 'The Indians continued to come and go on their nomadic excursions according to their habit, and while in this vicinity they lived in their wigwams near the river, their favorite camping place being at a point on the south bank near the present State Street bridge. A swale or gully opened into the river there, reaching back as far as the present line of Randolph Street. The movements of the Indians were regarded with great interest by the traders located in the neighborhood, who were anxious to sell them supplies in exchange for the furs brought in by them'. That families came and went to trade all year, and camped by the river near the creek's mouth while here, is Currey's; that some lodges stood there on any day is inferred from it.

levels.8-10: Currey wrote in 1912 that the Native people kept coming and going, as they always had. When they were near here, they lived in lodges by the river. Their favorite camp was on the south bank, near where the State Street bridge is now. A little stream ran into the river there, back to about where Randolph Street is now. The traders nearby watched for them. They wanted to trade goods for the furs the Native people brought. Currey tells us families came to trade all year and camped by the creek. That some lodges stood there on any one day is our guess.

entries.card: notes:FORTY FEET BY TWENTY-TWO, CITED TO NOTHING HERE. Du Sable's bill of sale of 1800 to Jean La Lime is reported to give the house as 22 by 40 feet (Quaife, 'Property of Jean Baptiste Point Sable', Mississippi Valley Historical Review 15:1, 1928, pp. 89-96), but that article is not in this corpus and was not read, so the figure stands as a reconstruction and the article is named only as what would replace it. It agrees with what the sources here do say: Wau-Bun's 'long, low building ... a range of four or five rooms' and every picture's long front, about twice as long as it is deep. The long side runs along the river.

It agrees with what the sources here do say: Wau-Bun's 'long, low building ... a range of four or five rooms' and every picture's long front, about twice as long as it is deep. The long side runs along the river.

levels.8-10: Forty feet by twenty-two. That size has no source here. An old article says Du Sable's bill of sale from 1800 gives the house as 22 by 40 feet. But we have not read that article, so the size is still a guess. It fits what our sources do say. Wau-Bun calls it a long, low house with four or five rooms in a row. Every picture shows a long front, about twice as long as the house is deep. The long side runs along the river.

The 1857 engraving puts one stack 0.45 of the ridge from the west gable and the other 0.93, by the east end; Lossing agrees on the middle one (0.4 from the west) and draws his second near the west gable (0.1). Three pictures of the four this ticket lists (the 1857 engraving, the Teich postcard at 0.43 and 0.81, the Cram plate's one stack at 0.93) put the second toward the east, so the 1857 engraving's places are built and Lossing's west stack is recorded in his match record as where the pictures disagree.

entries.card: notes:THE DRAWN OUTLINE, OPENED OUT WITH ITS PLACE. No scale is lettered at the field, so its box is opened by the bank's expansion: 30.998 x 18.166 m, about 560 square metres. The sheet's corners make a skewed quadrilateral and the archetype fences a rectangle, so the box stands for it: its length is the mean of the two drawn long sides, and its depth stops short of the drawn south-east side (108 of 141 px) so that the fence passes north of Le Mai's house, which the sheet draws outside the fence at that corner, by about 1.6 m. A field this size is small: the drafter compresses the ground outside the fort, and the size is as uncertain as the place (L-1812-coursoll-field-2513).

entries.card: notes:THE PATTERN IS THE LAW'S, NOT A DESCRIPTION. No source reached describes the first fort's colours; Quaife gives it 'a lofty flagstaff' at the parade's centre and a United States garrison flew the national flag. The Flag Act of 13 January 1794 made the flag fifteen stars and fifteen stripes from 1 May 1795, and it stayed so until the Act of 1818 took effect on 4 July 1818 - so every day of this phase (1803-1812) falls under it, Ohio's and Louisiana's admissions notwithstanding. The arrangement of the stars (five staggered rows of three), the size and the wear are reconstructed (L390).

levels.8-10: The flag's look comes from the law, not from anyone who saw it. No record tells us what the first fort's flag looked like. But an American fort flew the American flag. A law of 1794 said the flag had fifteen stars and fifteen stripes. That law lasted until 1818. So every day from 1803 to 1812 used that flag. How the stars were laid out, how big it was and how worn it was are our guesses.

entries.card: notes:THE RANGE IS INFERRED, NOT DATED FOR THIS FIELD. It opens on 25 January 1808, the date Whistler's draught carries, the one day a source shows the field fenced; it may well be older. That it still stood in August 1812 is continuity, not a reading: nothing in the corpus mentions it after the sheet, and Quaife finds the Courselles at Chicago otherwise only in Kinzie's account books. It closes on 16 August 1812 with the first fort, the day the post was burned and the people about it gone, as every part read by this rule does: a worm fence is stacked rails, and nothing says anybody kept this one through the four years the place stood empty. Closing it then keeps it out of every later scene and adds nothing to one.

levels.8-10: The years here are a guess. They start on 25 January 1808. That is the date on Whistler's drawing, the one day we know the field had a fence. It may be older. We guess it still stood in August 1812, but no record says so after the drawing. The Courselles show up at Chicago only in Kinzie's account books. The years end on 16 August 1812, when the fort burned and the people around it left. A worm fence is just a pile of rails. No one says anybody kept it up while the place stood empty for four years. So it ends then.

entries.card: notes:THE RANGE IS THE SCENE'S YEAR, NOT A DATE FOR THESE LODGES. Currey (ch. II, Gutenberg #52346 plain text lines 1360-1369) describes the Potawatomi coming and going to camp by the river in the years before the war, with no date for any lodge; the record stands for that habit, so it is drawn every day of 1812, whatever date the Season or a jaunt sets, beside the gathering's camps in August. entries.card: notes:THE SHEET DRAWS THE FIELD'S BOUND AS A DOTTED LINE, NOT AS A FENCE, so the fence is a reconstruction. It is the bounded one: a cornfield beside a cattle dealer's house and the garrison's hay meadow had to keep stock out, and the post's own field fence of these years is on record: Whistler had the picket fence north of the fort 'removed and replaced by a common rail fence' (Quaife 1913), and the draught letters the zigzag round Coursoll's field north of the river 'Worm Fence'. A common rail fence is a worm fence.

entries.card: notes:THE STACKS ARE DATED ONCE AND THE REST IS A BOUND THIS PROJECT CHOSE. Wau-Bun puts haystacks with the cattle on the bank opposite Lee's cabin on the afternoon the war party came, which it dates to the 7th of April 1812 (ch. XIX; Captain Heald's letter, cited on the cabin's record, gives the 6th) - the one day a source shows them. Those were the winter's stacks, fed from in April. The stacks standing on the 1812 scene's date are not the same hay: a farm that stacked on that bank in 1811 is taken to have cut and stacked there again in July 1812, and no source says whether anyone worked Lee's Place after April, so the stacks of the summer are reconstructed (L-1812-lees-place-haystacks-2510). They close on 16 August 1812, the day the post was burned: Charles Lee, his son and the rest of his household but his wife and infant fell on the 15th (Wau-Bun ch. XIX), and nothing was fed at Lee's Place after that.

entries.card: notes:The camp of the Potawatomi gathered at Chicago in August 1812, before the evacuation of the fort: Wau-Bun's 'Pottowattamie encampment' on the river's south bank (ch. XIX) and Currey's 'groups of Indian wigwams clustered along the creek' on 14 August (ch. III). Heald's letter says they came in for the goods of the factory store; Wau-Bun's council of the 12th was held with them. Whose lodges these were the sources do not say lodge by lodge — Wau-Bun names the wife of Wau-bee-nee-mah, 'a chief from the Illinois River', standing at one wigwam — and no lodge here is given to a family, a band or a person.

levels.8-10: The camp of the Potawatomi who came to Chicago in August 1812, before the soldiers left the fort. The book Wau-Bun tells of their camp on the south side of the river. Currey says groups of lodges stood along the creek on 14 August. Captain Heald wrote that they came for the goods in the fort's store. The meeting of the 12th was held with them. The old books do not say whose lodge was whose. Wau-Bun names one woman, the wife of a chief from the Illinois River, at one lodge. No lodge here is given to a family or a person.

entries.text: Wau-Bun ch. XVII describes 1831: 'a long, low building, with a piazza extending along its front'. Currey: Kinzie, after he bought it in 1804, 'repaired it, added a veranda'. Neither dates the veranda before August 1812; Lossing's view, which sets the house against the first fort, draws it, and that is the reading this phase takes.

levels.8-10: The book Wau-Bun tells of a long, low house with a porch along its front, in 1831. Currey says Kinzie bought the house in 1804, fixed it up and added a porch. Neither says the porch was there before August 1812. Lossing's picture shows the house next to the first fort with a porch. So the porch is built here.

levels.8-10: Whistler calls these three houses the Oather Dwelling Houses. That means other houses. Currey says this one was a plain little cabin. It was the home of Antoine Ouilmette.

entries.card: notes:Whistler's index lists '2 Port Holes for Cannon' and '3 Loop Holes for small arms' among the fort's features, and Quaife (after Wilson) puts the fort's cannon in the blockhouses. The register could not locate either numeral, so the slits' pattern and height are the archetype's.

levels.8-10: Whistler's list calls this number 11. It is on the west side. A writer named Quaife says the lower officers lived here. It was across from the other houses.

entries.card: notes:Whistler's index numbers its east room 12, 'Soldiers Barracks', and its west room 13, 'Contractors Store'. Quaife: 'The building opposite was in part devoted to barracks for the soldiers and in part to housing the contractor's store of supplies'. Built as one barracks range; the store is a room and the archetype builds no interiors.

entries.text: Black Partridge, Muck-otey-pokee in his own language, was a Potawatomi chief from the Illinois River, whose village stood on the south bank opposite the head of Peoria Lake. He had worn an American medal since General Wayne hung it on him at the Treaty of Greenville in 1795, and for seventeen years he kept faith with it.

levels.8-10: Black Partridge was a Potawatomi chief. In his own language his name was Muck-otey-pokee. His village was on the Illinois River, across from the top of Peoria Lake. In 1795 General Wayne gave him an American medal at a treaty meeting. For seventeen years he kept his word to the Americans.

entries.text: On the night of 14 August 1812 he walked into Captain Heald's quarters with the interpreter and gave the medal back. The young men, he said, could not be held; the 'linden birds' had been singing in his ears. The next morning, painted for war, he found seventeen-year-old Margaret Helm in the shallows of the lake, pulled her out of the fight and led her safe to the camp. On the 16th he sat as a guard on the Kinzies' porch, and he took Mrs. Lee and her baby home to his village.

levels.8-10: On the night of 14 August 1812 he went to see Captain Heald, with a man to turn his words into English. He gave the medal back. He said he could not hold back the young men. Birds had been singing in his ears, he said. The next morning he was painted for war. He found Margaret Helm, who was seventeen, in the water at the edge of the lake. He pulled her out of the fight and led her safely to the camp. On the 16th he sat on the Kinzies' porch to guard them. He took Mrs. Lee and her baby home to his village.

entries.text: His own village was destroyed in a single day in the war that followed. Andreas tells that he later bought Lieutenant Helm's freedom from the Kankakee with his pony, his rifle and the gold ring he wore in his nose.

levels.8-10: In the war that came next, his own village was wiped out in one day. A writer named Andreas tells that he later set Lieutenant Helm free. He paid the Kankakee people with his pony, his gun and the gold ring he wore in his nose.

entries.text: Black Bird, Mucketepennese to his own people and Letourneau to the French, was the Potawatomi war leader on 15 August 1812. That spring he was counted with Pepper's band on the Au Sable, and the year before he had sat in council with the Americans at Peoria.

levels.8-10: Black Bird was called Mucketepennese by his own people. The French called him Letourneau. He was the Potawatomi war leader on 15 August 1812. That spring he was counted with Pepper's band on the Au Sable River. The year before, he had met with the Americans at Peoria.

entries.text: When the fighting on the sand ridge was over, Captain Heald walked out alone toward the warriors. Black Bird came to meet him with an interpreter and asked him to surrender, promising that the prisoners' lives would be spared. Heald gave up. Quaife thought him the son of the chief who had helped the Americans raid St. Joseph in 1781.

levels.8-10: When the fight on the sand hill was over, Captain Heald walked out alone toward the warriors. Black Bird came to meet him, with a man to turn his words into English. He asked Heald to give up. He promised that the prisoners would not be killed. Heald gave up. A writer named Quaife thought Black Bird's father was the chief who helped the Americans attack St. Joseph in 1781.

entries.text: Thomas Burns had been a soldier at the fort, and when his time was up he stayed, building a house on the north bank near where the Indian agency would later stand. He married a widow, Mrs. Cooper, and took on her children as his own.

levels.8-10: Thomas Burns had been a soldier at the fort. When his time was done, he stayed. He built a house on the north bank of the river. He married a widow, Mrs. Cooper, and raised her children as his own.

entries.text: In April 1812, after the killings at Lee's farm, Heald enrolled the men of the settlement as militia, and Burns was made their sergeant. On 15 August he marched out with the twelve. He was badly wounded in the fight, and about an hour after the surrender he was killed where he lay.

levels.8-10: In April 1812 people were killed at Lee's farm. After that, Heald made the men of the town into a small army called the militia. Burns was put in charge of them, as their sergeant. On 15 August he marched out with the twelve men. He was badly hurt in the fight. About an hour after the Americans gave up, he was killed where he lay.

entries.text: Mrs. Burns had been Mrs. Cooper before she married Thomas Burns, and she brought a houseful of children to the house on the north bank. In April 1812, when word of the Lee farm killings sent everyone running for the fort, she had given birth only the day before; the Kinzies carried her down to the boat on her bed with the newborn in her arms.

levels.8-10: Mrs. Burns was once called Mrs. Cooper. Then she married Thomas Burns. She brought a house full of kids to his home on the north bank. In April 1812, people were killed at Lee's farm, and everyone ran to the fort. She had had a baby just the day before. The Kinzies carried her to the boat on her bed, with the new baby in her arms.

entries.text: On 15 August she lost her husband, her son Joseph and her two next-youngest children. She and her daughters were taken captive and spent two years among the Indians before traders bought them at Mackinac and sent them to Detroit. By 1820 she was living in Detroit, a widow keeping her three surviving children by her own work.

levels.8-10: On 15 August she lost her husband. She lost her son Joseph and two more of her kids too. She and her girls were taken prisoner. They lived with the Indians for two years. Then traders paid to get them back at Mackinac and sent them to Detroit. By 1820 she lived in Detroit. Her husband was gone, and she worked hard to raise her three kids who lived.

entries.text: Joseph Cooper (some accounts say James) was Mrs. Burns's son by her first marriage and Thomas Burns's stepson. When Heald formed a militia from the men of the settlement in April 1812, he joined his stepfather in it.

levels.8-10: Joseph Cooper was the son of Mrs. Burns from her first marriage. Some stories call him James. Thomas Burns was his stepdad. In April 1812 Heald made the men of the town into a small army called the militia. Joseph joined it with his stepdad.

entries.text: He marched with the militia on 15 August, and every one of the twelve was killed that morning, Joseph among them.

levels.8-10: On 15 August he marched out with the militia. All twelve of them were killed that morning. Joseph was one of them.

entries.text: Isabella Cooper was about nine years old in the summer of 1812, a daughter of Mrs. Burns by her first husband. On 15 August a warrior seized her, and though only a child she fought him with everything she had. She was scalped, and an old woman of the camp saved her life.

levels.8-10: Isabella Cooper was about nine in the summer of 1812. She was a daughter of Mrs. Burns from her first marriage. On 15 August a warrior grabbed her. She was only a child, but she fought back as hard as she could. She was badly hurt on her head. An old woman of the camp saved her life.

entries.text: She spent two years in captivity with her mother and sister. In 1816 she went to live with the Edwards family in Detroit, who remembered her at thirteen still carrying the scar. She grew up, married a man named Farnum, and lived many years in Detroit.

levels.8-10: She was a prisoner for two years with her mom and sister. In 1816 she went to live with the Edwards family in Detroit. They remembered that at thirteen she still had the scar. She grew up and married a man named Farnum. She lived in Detroit for many years.

entries.text: The Burns baby was born in April 1812, the day before the alarm that sent the whole settlement into the fort; she was carried to safety in her mother's arms, on her mother's bed, aboard the Kinzie boat.

levels.8-10: The Burns baby was born in April 1812. The very next day, everyone ran to the fort to be safe. Her mom held her on her bed as they carried them onto the Kinzie boat.

entries.text: In captivity after 15 August a tomahawk struck her and she lived. Twenty-two years later, on a steamboat, a young woman came up to Juliette Kinzie, said her name, lifted the hair from her forehead and showed the scar.

levels.8-10: After 15 August, when she was a prisoner, she was hit by a hatchet, and she lived. Twenty-two years later, a young woman walked up to Juliette Kinzie on a steamboat. She said her name. She lifted the hair from her forehead and showed the scar.

entries.text: On 15 August his wife, far along in pregnancy, was killed in the fighting. He was taken prisoner, and two years later he was one of the nine men of the garrison who came home by way of Quebec, reaching Plattsburg, New York, in May 1814.

entries.text: Mrs. Corbin was the wife of Private Fielding Corbin and lived with him at the fort. Wau-Bun remembers her as a woman who said from the first that she would never fall into the hands of the enemy.

entries.text: On 15 August, far advanced in pregnancy, she kept her word: she fought, refused to be taken, and was killed. A later tradition calls her Sukey Corbin, a washerwoman of the post, but even Kirkland, who printed it, trusted it less than the older accounts.

entries.text: Sergeant Otho Hays signed on in April 1811 and by every account of the fight was among the bravest men in Heald's company. Among the warriors who knew the fort was Nau-non-gee, a chief of the Calumet village, to whom Hays had shown many kindnesses.

levels.8-10: Otho Hays was a sergeant, a soldier in charge of other soldiers. He joined in April 1811. Every story of the fight says he was one of the bravest men in Heald's company. One of the warriors who knew the fort was Nau-non-gee, a chief from the Calumet village. Hays had been kind to him many times.

entries.text: On 15 August the two men met in the fight. As the story was first told by John Kinzie to Henry Schoolcraft in 1820, Hays drove his bayonet into the warrior's breast up to the socket, and in the same moment took the blow that killed him. Nau-non-gee died of the wound some days later at his village.

levels.8-10: On 15 August the two men met in the fight. John Kinzie first told the story to Henry Schoolcraft in 1820. He said each man gave the other a deadly wound at the same moment. Hays died there. Nau-non-gee died a few days later at his village.

entries.text: Sergeant John Crozier had served at Fort Dearborn since July 1808, one of the old hands of the company.

levels.8-10: John Crozier was a sergeant, a soldier in charge of other soldiers. He had been at Fort Dearborn since July 1808. He was one of the old hands of the company.

entries.text: He survived the fight on 15 August and was led off a prisoner to the Au Sable River. There a Chippewa man, an old friend of his, took him away to Green Bay and so set him free. Lieutenant Helm, writing his list of survivors, wrongly marked him a deserter; Crozier was among the sergeants alive at Detroit that autumn.

levels.8-10: He lived through the fight on 15 August. He was taken as a prisoner to the Au Sable River. There a Chippewa man, an old friend, took him away to Green Bay and set him free. Lieutenant Helm made a list of the soldiers who lived. By mistake, he wrote that Crozier had run away. But Crozier was one of the sergeants alive at Detroit that fall.

entries.text: William Griffith was a civilian of the settlement until the killings at Lee's farm in April 1812; on 1 May he enlisted at Chicago itself and was soon a sergeant. It was Griffith who later told how Black Partridge warned that the 'linden birds' had been singing in his ears.

levels.8-10: William Griffith lived in the town. He was not a soldier until April 1812, when people were killed at Lee's farm. On 1 May he joined the army right here at Chicago. Soon he was a sergeant. Later it was Griffith who told how Black Partridge gave a warning. Birds had been singing in his ears, the chief said.

entries.text: On 15 August Topenebe, the St. Joseph chief, took him prisoner and then let him hide. Griffith escaped with Captain and Mrs. Heald by canoe to Mackinac and travelled home with them by Detroit and Pittsburgh. Eight years later he wrote to Heald to help Mrs. Burns win her widow's pension.

levels.8-10: On 15 August Topenebe, the chief from St. Joseph, took him prisoner. Then he let Griffith hide. Griffith got away by canoe to Mackinac with Captain and Mrs. Heald. He went home with them by way of Detroit and Pittsburgh. Eight years later he wrote to Heald. He wanted to help Mrs. Burns get money from the army, since her husband had died.

entries.text: In August 1812 General Hull ordered him to give up the post.
