entries.text: A second of John Kinzie's engagés, a French Canadian or Métis hired man of the trading house, whose name no one recorded. Wau-Bun speaks of 'the boatmen' in the Kinzie boat on 15 August, and the lodging house 'for the Frenchmen' held more than one.

levels.8-10: He was another of John Kinzie's hired men. He came from French Canada, or was part French and part Indian. No one wrote down his name. The book Wau-Bun talks about "the boatmen" in the Kinzie boat on 15 August. The house for the Frenchmen held more than one man.

entries.text: Like the other engagés he wintered at an outpost and came in with the furs in spring. On 15 August he was with the family in the boat, and on the 18th he helped carry them to St. Joseph.

levels.8-10: Like the other hired men, he spent the winter far out, and came back with the furs in the spring. On 15 August he was with the family in the boat. On the 18th he helped take them to St. Joseph.

entries.text: John Kinzie was born in Quebec in 1763 and learned the silversmith's trade before he took to the Indian trade. He came to Chicago about 1804 and took the old house on the north bank of the river, facing the fort, and grew to be the most important trader of the place.

levels.8-10: John Kinzie was born in Quebec in 1763. First he learned to make things out of silver. Then he started trading with the Indians. He came to Chicago around 1804. He took the old house on the north bank of the river, across from the fort. He grew to be the most important trader there.

entries.text: He knew everyone, and everyone knew him. He interpreted at Heald's council with the chiefs on 12 August 1812. Two months earlier, on the evening of 17 June, he had fought the government interpreter Jean Lalime outside the fort's gate and killed him, and a friend took him to Milwaukee that night until it was safe to come back.

levels.8-10: He knew everyone, and everyone knew him. On 12 August 1812, Heald met with the chiefs, and Kinzie turned their words into English. Two months before, on the evening of 17 June, he had fought Jean Lalime outside the fort's gate. Lalime turned Indian words into English for the army. Kinzie killed him. A friend took Kinzie to Milwaukee that night, until it was safe to come back.

entries.text: On 15 August, warned by Topenebe, he put his family in the boat and marched out with the soldiers himself. His friends among the chiefs kept him alive, and in the days after he and his family were spared and taken to St. Joseph and Detroit.

levels.8-10: On 15 August Topenebe warned him what was coming. Kinzie put his family in the boat. Then he marched out with the soldiers himself. His friends among the chiefs kept him alive. In the days after, he and his family were spared. They were taken to St. Joseph and Detroit.

entries.text: Eleanor Kinzie, born Eleanor Lytle, had been a widow, Mrs. McKillip, with a daughter, Margaret, when she married John Kinzie about 1800. She had four children by him and ran the household in the big house across the river.

levels.8-10: Eleanor Kinzie was born Eleanor Lytle. Her first husband had died. She was Mrs. McKillip then, and she had a daughter, Margaret. Around 1800 she married John Kinzie. They had four children. She ran the big house across the river.

entries.text: From April 1812 the family lived inside the fort. On the morning of 15 August she sat in the boat at the river mouth with her four younger children and their nurse, and watched her husband and her eldest daughter march away with the column. They came back to her alive. After three anxious days at the house across the river, the family went to St. Joseph and then to Detroit as prisoners of war.

levels.8-10: From April 1812 the family lived inside the fort. On the morning of 15 August she sat in the boat at the mouth of the river. Her four younger kids and their nurse were with her. She watched her husband and her oldest daughter march away with the soldiers. They both came back to her alive. The family spent three worried days at the house across the river. Then they were taken to St. Joseph and Detroit as prisoners of war.

entries.text: John Harris Kinzie, born at Sandwich in Canada in July 1803, was nine years old in the summer of 1812, the eldest of John and Eleanor Kinzie's children.

levels.8-10: John Harris Kinzie was born at Sandwich, in Canada, in July 1803. In the summer of 1812 he was nine. He was the oldest child of John and Eleanor Kinzie.
levels.11-13: John Harris Kinzie was born at Sandwich, in Canada, in July 1803. He was nine in the summer of 1812, the oldest child of John and Eleanor Kinzie.

entries.text: On 15 August he sat in the family boat at the river mouth with his mother, sisters and baby brother while the battle was fought down the shore, and he went with the family to St. Joseph and Detroit. He grew up to be an Indian agent and a founder of the city of Chicago, and his wife Juliette wrote Wau-Bun, the book that told the family's story.

levels.8-10: On 15 August he sat in the family boat at the mouth of the river. His mom, his sisters and his baby brother were with him. The fight went on down the shore. He went with the family to St. Joseph and Detroit. When he grew up, he worked with the Indians for the government. He helped start the city of Chicago. His wife, Juliette, wrote a book called Wau-Bun. It told the family's story.
levels.11-13: On 15 August he sat in the family boat at the river mouth with his mother, sisters and baby brother, while the battle was fought down the shore. He went with the family to St. Joseph and Detroit. He grew up to be an Indian agent and one of the founders of the city of Chicago. His wife Juliette wrote Wau-Bun, the book that told the family's story.

entries.text: Ellen Marion Kinzie was born in Chicago in December 1805, among the first children born to a family settled there, and was six and a half in the summer of 1812.

levels.8-10: Ellen Marion Kinzie was born in Chicago in December 1805. She was one of the first children born to a family that lived there. In the summer of 1812 she was six and a half.

entries.text: She was in the boat with her mother on 15 August and went with the family to St. Joseph and Detroit. She grew up to marry Dr. Alexander Wolcott, the Indian agent at Chicago.

levels.8-10: She was in the boat with her mom on 15 August. She went with the family to St. Joseph and Detroit. When she grew up, she married Dr. Alexander Wolcott. He worked with the Indians at Chicago for the government.

entries.text: Maria Indiana Kinzie was born in Chicago in 1807 and was about four years old in the summer of 1812.

levels.8-10: Maria Indiana Kinzie was born in Chicago in 1807. In the summer of 1812 she was about four.

entries.text: She was in the boat with her mother on 15 August and went with the family to St. Joseph and Detroit. She grew up to marry David Hunter, later a general in the Civil War.

levels.8-10: She was in the boat with her mom on 15 August. She went with the family to St. Joseph and Detroit. When she grew up, she married David Hunter. Later he was a general in the Civil War.

entries.text: Robert Allen Kinzie was born on 8 February 1810, the baby of the family, two and a half years old in the summer of 1812.

levels.8-10: Robert Allen Kinzie was born on 8 February 1810. He was the baby of the family. In the summer of 1812 he was two and a half.

entries.text: He was in his mother's arms in the boat on 15 August and went with the family to St. Joseph and Detroit. He came back to Chicago as a young man and traded there in the 1830s.

levels.8-10: He was in his mom's arms in the boat on 15 August. He went with the family to St. Joseph and Detroit. He came back to Chicago as a young man. He traded there in the 1830s.

entries.text: Josette LaFramboise, a young woman of French and Ottawa family, was nurse to the Kinzie children. (Wau-Bun's printer turned her name into 'Grutte'.)

levels.8-10: Josette LaFramboise was a young woman. Her family was French and Ottawa. She was the nurse who cared for the Kinzie kids. (The man who printed Wau-Bun got her name wrong. He called her Grutte.)

entries.text: On 15 August she sat in the boat with Mrs. Kinzie and the children while the battle was fought. Soon after, in 1812 or 1814 depending on the account, she married Jean Baptiste Beaubien, and as Madame Beaubien she raised a large family in the Chicago of the 1830s.

levels.8-10: On 15 August she sat in the boat with Mrs. Kinzie and the kids while the fight went on. Soon after, she married Jean Baptiste Beaubien. Some stories say it was in 1812, and some say 1814. As Madame Beaubien, she raised a big family in Chicago in the 1830s.

entries.text: Jean Baptiste Chandonnai was John Kinzie's clerk, a young man of French and Potawatomi family who moved easily between the trading house and the camps. On 15 August Kinzie put his family in Chandonnai's care in the boat.

levels.8-10: Jean Baptiste Chandonnai was John Kinzie's clerk. He was a young man from a French and Potawatomi family. He was at home both in the trading house and in the camps. On 15 August Kinzie left his family in Chandonnai's care in the boat.

entries.text: That same day he saved Rebekah Heald. Wounded and in a warrior's hands, she was about to be killed when Chandonnai bought her life with a mule and a promise of whiskey and brought her back to her husband; he then escorted the Healds toward St. Joseph. Every account of the day credits him with tireless efforts to save the prisoners.

levels.8-10: That same day he saved Rebekah Heald. She was hurt, and a warrior was about to kill her. Chandonnai paid for her life with a mule and a promise of whiskey. He brought her back to her husband. Then he took the Healds toward St. Joseph. Every story of that day says he worked and worked to save the prisoners.

entries.text: That fall he took Mrs. Kinzie and the children to Detroit. He was back in Kinzie's employ by about 1816, traded at Chicago and beyond, and at the treaty of 1821 was granted two sections of land.

levels.8-10: That fall he took Mrs. Kinzie and the kids to Detroit. By about 1816 he was working for Kinzie again. He traded at Chicago and farther away. At the treaty of 1821 he was given two big pieces of land.

entries.text: Pierre Le Clerc, 'Peresh' in Wau-Bun, was a young man of French and Indian family in John Kinzie's service, who had lived for years a few yards from the fort. By one tradition it was he who brought the news of war to Chicago in July.

levels.8-10: Pierre Le Clerc worked for John Kinzie. The book Wau-Bun calls him Peresh. He was a young man from a French and Indian family. He had lived a few steps from the fort for years. One story says he was the one who brought the news of war to Chicago in July.

entries.text: On 15 August he marched with the soldiers and fought on their side; then, at Helm's word, he went over to the warriors and carried the terms of surrender between the two sides. He survived, and at the treaty of 1821 was granted a section of land on the Elkhart.

levels.8-10: On 15 August he marched with the soldiers and fought on their side. Then Helm asked him to go over to the warriors. He carried the words about giving up back and forth between the two sides. He lived. At the treaty of 1821 he was given a piece of land on the Elkhart River.

entries.text: Jean Lalime was the government's interpreter at Fort Dearborn, a Frenchman of some education who had wintered at Chicago since 1803 and lived in one of the log houses on the north bank. The fort's doctor called him 'a very decent man and a good companion', and his letters to Fort Wayne passed on what the Indians were saying.

levels.8-10: Jean Lalime worked for the army at Fort Dearborn. He turned Indian words into English. He was a Frenchman who had gone to school. He spent winters at Chicago from 1803, in one of the log houses on the north bank. The fort's doctor called him a very nice man and a good friend. His letters to Fort Wayne passed on what the Indians were saying.

entries.text: At sunset on 17 June 1812, as the fort's gate was being shut, he and John Kinzie met just outside it and fought; Kinzie came away with a wound in his neck and Lalime lay dead. He was buried near the Kinzie house, in full view of its porch, inside a picket fence.

levels.8-10: At sunset on 17 June 1812, the fort's gate was being shut. He and John Kinzie met just outside it and fought. Kinzie was cut on the neck, and Lalime was killed. He was buried near the Kinzie house, inside a fence, where people on the porch could see.

entries.text: Charles Lee settled at Chicago about 1805 and is said to have held the contract to supply the garrison with provisions. His farm on the South Branch, Lee's Place, later called Hardscrabble, fed the fort, and his family lived in a house near the river mouth.

levels.8-10: Charles Lee came to live at Chicago around 1805. People say he had the job of bringing food to the soldiers. His farm was on the South Branch of the river. It was called Lee's Place, and later Hardscrabble. It fed the fort. His family lived in a house near the mouth of the river.

entries.text: On 6 April 1812 a war party killed the two men working the farm, and the whole settlement fled into the fort. Lee joined the militia Heald formed that spring, and on 15 August he and his son were killed with the rest of the twelve.

levels.8-10: On 6 April 1812 a war party killed the two men working on the farm. Everyone in the town ran into the fort. That spring Lee joined the small army of town men, called the militia. On 15 August he and his son were killed with the rest of the twelve.

entries.text: Mrs. Lee lived with her husband Charles and their children in the house near the river mouth. On 15 August she lost her husband, her son and her twelve-year-old daughter, and with her baby she was taken captive by Black Partridge to his village.

levels.8-10: Mrs. Lee lived with her husband, Charles, and their kids in the house near the mouth of the river. On 15 August she lost her husband, her son, and her daughter, who was twelve. Black Partridge took her and her baby to his village as prisoners.

entries.text: That winter the trader Du Pin bought her and her child back at Chicago, and in time Mrs. Lee became Madame Du Pin. She is said to have sold the Lee house to Jean Baptiste Beaubien.

levels.8-10: That winter a trader named Du Pin paid to get her and her baby back at Chicago. In time Mrs. Lee married him and became Madame Du Pin. People say she sold the Lee house to Jean Baptiste Beaubien.

entries.text: Lee's daughter was about twelve in the summer of 1812, and Black Partridge was especially fond of her.

levels.8-10: The Lees' daughter was about twelve in the summer of 1812. Black Partridge was very fond of her.

entries.text: On 15 August she rode out on horseback with the column. Wau-Bun tells that she was badly wounded, and that Black Partridge, unable to save her, ended her suffering himself.

levels.8-10: On 15 August she rode out on a horse with the soldiers. The book Wau-Bun says she was badly hurt. Black Partridge could not save her. So he ended her pain himself.

entries.text: The Lees' baby, the youngest of the family, whose name no record keeps.

levels.8-10: This was the Lees' baby, the youngest of the family. No record keeps the baby's name.

entries.text: Taken captive with its mother on 15 August, the baby fell ill among the Indians but lived, and was ransomed with her at Chicago that winter.

levels.8-10: The baby was taken prisoner with its mom on 15 August. The baby got sick but lived. That winter someone paid to get them both back at Chicago.

entries.text: Liberty White was an American who had lived at Chicago for some time and had charge of Charles Lee's farm on the South Branch.

levels.8-10: Liberty White was an American. He had lived at Chicago for a while. He was in charge of Charles Lee's farm on the South Branch of the river.
levels.11-13: Liberty White was an American who had lived at Chicago for some time. He was in charge of Charles Lee's farm on the South Branch.

entries.text: A little before sunset on 6 April 1812 a party of strangers who had come to the farm killed him and the Canadian Jean Baptiste Cardin. His body was found pierced by two balls and stabbed eleven times, and the news sent every family in the settlement into the fort.

levels.8-10: On 6 April 1812, a little before sunset, some strangers came to the farm. They killed him and a Canadian man, Jean Baptiste Cardin. The news sent every family in the town running into the fort.
levels.11-13: A little before sunset on 6 April 1812, a party of strangers who had come to the farm killed him and the Canadian Jean Baptiste Cardin. His body had been shot twice and stabbed many times. The news sent every family in the town into the fort.

entries.text: Jean Baptiste Cardin was a Canadian who had only lately come to Chicago and was working on Lee's farm in the spring of 1812. Watching the party of visitors who came to the farm that April day, he said he could tell by their dress and paint that they were not Potawatomi.

levels.8-10: Jean Baptiste Cardin came from Canada. He had come to Chicago not long before. In the spring of 1812 he worked on Lee's farm. One April day some visitors came to the farm. He said he could tell from their clothes and face paint that they were not Potawatomi.

entries.text: He was right to be uneasy. A little before sunset on 6 April they killed him and Liberty White.

levels.8-10: He was right to be worried. A little before sunset on 6 April, they killed him and Liberty White.

entries.text: Fox Running was a runner sent from Main Poc, the Potawatomi war leader who had gone over to the British.

levels.8-10: Fox Running was a runner. He was sent by Main Poc, a Potawatomi war leader who had joined the British.

entries.text: He came into the camp at Chicago on 14 August 1812 carrying a large red belt, the sign of war, and news of British victories in the north.

levels.8-10: He came into the camp at Chicago on 14 August 1812. He carried a big red belt. It was the sign of war. He brought news that the British were winning up north.

entries.text: Jean Baptiste Mirandeau was a Frenchman married to an Ottawa woman; his daughter remembered him as a good scholar, a very handsome man, with many books. He was among the first settlers at Milwaukee.

levels.8-10: Jean Baptiste Mirandeau was a Frenchman. His wife was Ottawa. His daughter remembered him as a smart and very handsome man with lots of books. He was one of the first people to settle at Milwaukee.

entries.text: In 1811 he came down to Chicago and did blacksmith work at the fort, lodging his family in the Ouilmette house across the river. On the night of 17 June 1812, after John Kinzie killed Lalime, Mirandeau packed up some things and took Kinzie to Milwaukee. The family went home too, and were gone before the fort burned.

levels.8-10: In 1811 he came down to Chicago and worked as a blacksmith at the fort. His family stayed in the Ouilmette house across the river. On the night of 17 June 1812, John Kinzie killed Lalime. Mirandeau packed a few things and took Kinzie to Milwaukee. His family went home too. They were gone before the fort burned.

entries.text: Victoire Mirandeau, born about 1800, was a daughter of the blacksmith Jean Baptiste Mirandeau and his Ottawa wife. She grew up speaking French and her mother's language, and never learned to read or write.

levels.8-10: Victoire Mirandeau was born around 1800. Her dad was the blacksmith Jean Baptiste Mirandeau. Her mom was Ottawa. She grew up speaking French and her mom's language. She never learned to read or write.

entries.text: In 1811 the family came down from Milwaukee and lodged at the Ouilmette house while her father worked at the fort. At sunset on 17 June 1812, as the gates were being shut, she and her sister Madeline watched John Kinzie and Lalime fight. That night her father took Kinzie to Milwaukee, and the family followed. Years later she lived with the Kinzies as their servant.

levels.8-10: In 1811 the family came down from Milwaukee. They stayed at the Ouilmette house while her dad worked at the fort. At sunset on 17 June 1812, the gates were being shut. She and her sister Madeline watched John Kinzie and Lalime fight. That night her dad took Kinzie to Milwaukee, and the family went too. Years later she lived with the Kinzies and worked for them.

entries.text: Madeline Mirandeau was a daughter of the blacksmith Jean Baptiste Mirandeau and his Ottawa wife, and later the wife of John K. Clark.

levels.8-10: Madeline Mirandeau was a daughter of the blacksmith. His name was Jean Baptiste Mirandeau. Her mom was Ottawa. Later she married John K. Clark.

entries.text: She was lodging at the Ouilmette house with her family while her father worked at the fort, and at sunset on 17 June 1812 she and her sister Victoire saw the fight between John Kinzie and Lalime. The family left that night. She lived at Chicago before the massacre and after it, though not at the time.

levels.8-10: She stayed at the Ouilmette house with her family while her dad worked at the fort. At sunset on 17 June 1812, she and her sister Victoire saw John Kinzie and Lalime fight. The family left that night. She lived at Chicago before the big fight and after it, but not when it happened.

entries.text: Nau-non-gee was one of the chiefs of the Calumet village south of Chicago. That spring, Wau-Bun remembers, he watched the officers' wives at play and remarked that they were amusing themselves very much, and that it would not be long before they were hoeing in his cornfield.

levels.8-10: Nau-non-gee was one of the chiefs of the Calumet village, south of Chicago. The book Wau-Bun remembers something he said that spring. He watched the officers' wives playing. He said they were having lots of fun. But soon, he said, they would be hoeing in his cornfield.

entries.text: On 15 August he sought out Sergeant Otho Hays, a man who had shown him many kindnesses. They fought; Hays drove his bayonet into his breast in the same moment he fell. Nau-non-gee was carried home and died of the wound some days later.

levels.8-10: On 15 August he looked for Sergeant Otho Hays, a man who had been kind to him many times. They fought. Each gave the other a deadly wound at the same moment. Nau-non-gee was carried home. He died a few days later.

entries.text: Private John Needs, formerly of Virginia, enlisted in July 1808 and lived at the fort with his wife and their child.

levels.8-10: John Needs was a private, the plainest kind of soldier. He came from Virginia. He joined in July 1808. He lived at the fort with his wife and their child.

entries.text: He survived the fight on 15 August, but the captivity killed him: he died among the Indians in the middle of January 1813. His wife and child died too.

levels.8-10: He lived through the fight on 15 August. But he died as a prisoner, in the middle of January 1813. His wife and child died too.

entries.text: Nuscotnemeg, the Mad Sturgeon, was a Potawatomi war leader already blamed for killings in Illinois in 1810. His daughter was Billy Caldwell's wife.

levels.8-10: Nuscotnemeg was called the Mad Sturgeon. He was a Potawatomi war leader. People already blamed him for killings in Illinois in 1810. His daughter was Billy Caldwell's wife.

entries.text: He was among the attackers on 15 August and was badly wounded; by the next day his friends were carrying him off toward the Des Plaines. He recovered, and in 1817 a traveller named Storrow met him at Chicago.

levels.8-10: He was one of the attackers on 15 August. He was badly hurt. By the next day his friends were carrying him off toward the Des Plaines River. He got well. In 1817 a traveler named Storrow met him at Chicago.

entries.text: Antoine Ouilmette was a French Canadian who claimed to have come to Chicago in 1790, before the fort; he was living with his Potawatomi wife Archange in one of the four log houses when the soldiers arrived in 1803. He worked for John Kinzie, carrying goods over the portage.

levels.8-10: Antoine Ouilmette came from French Canada. He said he came to Chicago in 1790, before there was a fort. His wife, Archange, was Potawatomi. When the soldiers came in 1803, they lived in one of the four log houses. He worked for John Kinzie. He carried goods over the land between the rivers.

entries.text: He never joined the militia, and when the garrison marched out he simply stayed home. After the Kinzie boat left on the 18th he was the only white man left at Chicago, and he was still there, living in serene possession, when the new garrison came in 1816. In 1829 his wife was granted land at Gros Point, where the town of Wilmette now takes his name.

levels.8-10: He never joined the militia. When the soldiers marched out, he just stayed home. The Kinzie boat left on the 18th. After that he was the only white man left at Chicago. He was still there, living calmly, when new soldiers came in 1816. In 1829 his wife was given land at Gros Point. The town there, Wilmette, is named after him.

entries.text: Archange Ouilmette, Okra in one account, was a Potawatomi woman married to Antoine Ouilmette, and the household she ran on the north bank was part of the Kinzie establishment.

levels.8-10: Archange Ouilmette was a Potawatomi woman. One story calls her Okra. She was married to Antoine Ouilmette. The house she ran on the north bank was part of the Kinzie place.

entries.text: On the morning of 15 August she watched from beside her house as the troops marched out along the shore. Her family stayed through all that followed. In 1829 a treaty granted her and her children land, and she later went west with her people and died at Council Bluffs.

levels.8-10: On the morning of 15 August she stood by her house and watched the soldiers march out along the shore. Her family stayed through all that came after. In 1829 a treaty gave her and her children land. Later she went west with her people. She died at Council Bluffs.

entries.text: Mrs. Bisson was Archange Ouilmette's sister and lived in the Ouilmette household on the north bank.

levels.8-10: Mrs. Bisson was Archange Ouilmette's sister. She lived in the Ouilmette house on the north bank.

entries.text: In the story the Kinzie family told, on 16 August she hid Margaret Helm in the Ouilmette house, sitting calmly on the bed with her sewing while warriors searched the room.

levels.8-10: The Kinzie family told this story. On 16 August she hid Margaret Helm in the Ouilmette house. Warriors came and searched the room. She sat calmly on the bed, sewing, the whole time.

entries.text: The children of Antoine and Archange Ouilmette, who grew up in the house on the north bank speaking French and Potawatomi. Their names, Elizabeth, Michell, Lewis, Francis, Sophie, Joseph and later Josette, were written down only long afterwards.

levels.8-10: These are the children of Antoine and Archange Ouilmette. They grew up in the house on the north bank. They spoke French and Potawatomi. Their names were Elizabeth, Michell, Lewis, Francis, Sophie, Joseph and, later, Josette. No one wrote the names down until long after.
levels.11-13: These are the children of Antoine and Archange Ouilmette. They grew up in the house on the north bank, speaking French and Potawatomi. Their names were Elizabeth, Michell, Lewis, Francis, Sophie, Joseph and, later, Josette. They were written down only long afterwards.

entries.text: They stayed at Chicago with their parents through the massacre and the war, among the very few who did, and as grown people went west with the Potawatomi to Kansas.

levels.8-10: They stayed at Chicago with their mom and dad through the massacre and the war. Very few people did that. When they grew up, they went west to Kansas with the Potawatomi.
levels.11-13: They stayed at Chicago with their parents through the massacre and the war. They were among the very few who did. As grown-ups they went west with the Potawatomi to Kansas.

entries.text: Pee-so-tum was a Potawatomi warrior at the gathering of August 1812.

levels.8-10: Pee-so-tum was a Potawatomi warrior. He was at the big gathering in August 1812.

entries.text: Margaret Helm remembered him leading her toward the lodges after the fight, a scalp hanging from his hand that she knew by its black ribbon for Captain Wells's.

levels.8-10: After the fight, he led Margaret Helm toward the lodges. She remembered what he held in his hand. She knew by its black ribbon that it was from Captain Wells, and that Wells was dead.

entries.text: Alexander Robinson, Che-che-pin-qua, was a trader from St. Joseph, born at Mackinac to an Odawa mother and a Scottish father. Whether he was at Chicago on 15 August the old accounts argue; all agree on what he did after.

levels.8-10: Alexander Robinson was also called Che-che-pin-qua. He was a trader from St. Joseph. He was born at Mackinac. His mom was Odawa and his dad was from Scotland. The old stories argue about whether he was at Chicago on 15 August. They all agree on what he did after.
levels.11-13: Alexander Robinson, called Che-che-pin-qua, was a trader from St. Joseph. He was born at Mackinac to an Odawa mother and a Scottish father. The old accounts argue about whether he was at Chicago on 15 August. They all agree on what he did after.

entries.text: At St. Joseph he sheltered the Kinzies, and with his wife he paddled the wounded Healds all the way to Mackinac. He later became a chief of the united Potawatomi, Chippewa and Ottawa, signed the treaty of 1833, kept a reservation on the Des Plaines, and died there in 1872.

levels.8-10: At St. Joseph he took care of the Kinzies. He and his wife paddled the hurt Healds all the way to Mackinac. Later he became a chief of the Potawatomi, Chippewa and Ottawa together. He signed the treaty of 1833. He kept some land on the Des Plaines River, and he died there in 1872.
levels.11-13: At St. Joseph he sheltered the Kinzies. With his wife, he paddled the wounded Healds all the way to Mackinac. He later became a chief of the united Potawatomi, Chippewa and Ottawa. He signed the treaty of 1833, kept land on the Des Plaines River, and died there in 1872.

entries.text: Ensign George Ronan came straight from West Point in March 1811, the youngest officer at Fort Dearborn. His signature survives on an order of November 1811 allowing the men a gill of whiskey each.

levels.8-10: George Ronan was an ensign, the lowest kind of officer. He came straight from West Point, the army's school, in March 1811. He was the youngest officer at Fort Dearborn. His name is on an order from November 1811. It gave each man a small cup of whiskey.

entries.text: On 15 August he was killed near the baggage wagons. Wau-Bun says he fought to the last on one knee.

levels.8-10: On 15 August he was killed near the wagons. The book Wau-Bun says he kept fighting to the end, down on one knee.

entries.text: Shabbona was an Ottawa by birth who married into a Potawatomi band of the Illinois River and became its leader; in 1812 he was an aide to Tecumseh.

levels.8-10: Shabbona was born Ottawa. He married into a Potawatomi band of the Illinois River and became its leader. In 1812 he was a helper to Tecumseh.
levels.11-13: Shabbona was born Ottawa. He married into a Potawatomi band of the Illinois River and became its leader. In 1812 he was a helper to Tecumseh.

entries.text: By his own account he set out for Chicago when he heard the warriors had gone there, and came in with twenty-two men a few hours after the fight, standing that night among the guards around the Kinzie house. He signed the treaty of 1816 that gave up the land around Chicago, kept the peace in 1832, was granted land at Shabbona Grove and lost it, and died near Morris, Illinois, in 1859.

entries.text: Private John Simmons enlisted in March 1810 and lived at the fort with his wife Susan and their two children, David, about two, and baby Susan, born at the fort in February 1812.

levels.8-10: John Simmons was a private, the plainest kind of soldier. He joined in March 1810. He lived at the fort with his wife, Susan, and their two kids. David was about two. Baby Susan was born at the fort in February 1812.

entries.text: On 15 August he was one of the little band of soldiers who died fighting around the baggage wagons. His son David was killed in the children's wagon.

levels.8-10: On 15 August he was one of a small group of soldiers who died fighting around the wagons. His son David was killed in the children's wagon.

entries.text: Susan Millhouse Simmons was a Pennsylvanian, the wife of Private John Simmons, who lived with him at the fort with their son David and their baby daughter.

levels.8-10: Susan Millhouse Simmons came from Pennsylvania. She was married to John Simmons, a soldier. She lived with him at the fort, with their son David and their baby girl.

entries.text: On 15 August she lost her husband and her son. Carrying her baby, she walked with her captors to Green Bay, back by Chicago to Mackinac, and on to Detroit, and in April 1813 at last reached her parents near Piqua, Ohio. She died in Springville, Iowa, in 1857.

levels.8-10: On 15 August she lost her husband and her son. She carried her baby and walked with the people who held her prisoner. They went to Green Bay, back past Chicago to Mackinac, and on to Detroit. In April 1813 she finally got to her mom and dad's home near Piqua, Ohio. She died in Springville, Iowa, in 1857.

entries.text: Susan Simmons was born at Fort Dearborn in February 1812, the daughter of Private John Simmons and his wife Susan.

levels.8-10: Susan Simmons was born at Fort Dearborn in February 1812. Her dad was John Simmons, a soldier. Her mom was also named Susan.

entries.text: Six months old on 15 August, she was carried by her mother through the whole captivity and home to Ohio. She lived to be the last survivor of the Fort Dearborn massacre, dying at Santa Ana, California, on 27 April 1900.

levels.8-10: On 15 August she was six months old. Her mom carried her the whole time they were prisoners, and all the way home to Ohio. She lived longer than anyone else who was there that day. She died at Santa Ana, California, on 27 April 1900.

entries.text: Topenebe was the principal chief of the St. Joseph band of Potawatomi and a friend of the Kinzies for many years; his sister KawKeemee married the trader William Burnett.

levels.8-10: Topenebe was the top chief of the St. Joseph band of Potawatomi. He had been a friend of the Kinzies for many years. His sister, KawKeemee, married a trader named William Burnett.

entries.text: Early on 15 August he sent word to John Kinzie of what was coming. He held the Kinzie boat at the river mouth to keep the family out of the fight, took Sergeant Griffith prisoner and then let him hide, and sheltered the Kinzies at St. Joseph until November. At the treaty of 1821 he was nearly eighty years old.

levels.8-10: Early on 15 August he sent word to John Kinzie about what was coming. He kept the Kinzie boat at the mouth of the river, so the family stayed out of the fight. He took Sergeant Griffith prisoner and then let him hide. He kept the Kinzies safe at St. Joseph until November. At the treaty of 1821 he was almost eighty.

entries.text: Isaac Van Voorhis, of Fishkill, New York, was the fort's surgeon's mate, a young doctor of twenty-two when he wrote home in 1811 about the country and its prospects. When the factor Irwin left in July 1812, he held the keys of the government trading house.

levels.8-10: Isaac Van Voorhis came from Fishkill, New York. He was the fort's young doctor. In 1811 he was twenty-two. That year he wrote home about the land and how it might grow. When Irwin left in July 1812, Van Voorhis kept the keys to the government store.

entries.text: On 15 August he was killed near the baggage wagons.

levels.8-10: On 15 August he was killed near the wagons.

entries.text: Wau-bee-nee-mah was a Potawatomi chief from the Illinois River whose lodge stood in the camp by the creek.

levels.8-10: Wau-bee-nee-mah was a Potawatomi chief from the Illinois River. His lodge stood in the camp by the creek.

entries.text: When Margaret Helm was brought to the camp on 15 August, he stretched a mat between two poles to hide from her the killing of a wounded prisoner.

levels.8-10: On 15 August Margaret Helm was brought to the camp. A hurt prisoner was being killed there. The chief hung a mat between two poles so she would not have to see it.

entries.text: Rain After Thunder was the wife of Wau-bee-nee-mah, a woman of the Illinois River band; Wau-Bun gives her no name of her own, and this one is ours.

levels.8-10: Rain After Thunder was the wife of Wau-bee-nee-mah. She was from the Illinois River band. The book Wau-Bun does not give her a name. We gave her this one.

entries.text: When Margaret Helm was brought to the camp on 15 August, shaking and parched, this woman took a kettle, dipped water from the stream, stirred in maple sugar with her hand and gave it to her to drink.

levels.8-10: On 15 August Margaret Helm was brought to the camp. She was shaking and very thirsty. This woman took a kettle and got water from the stream. She stirred in maple sugar with her hand and gave it to her to drink.

entries.text: William Wells was born in Kentucky, captured by the Miami as a boy, adopted by them, and married to a daughter of their great war chief Little Turtle. He had fought on both sides of the Indian wars and was the Indian agent at Fort Wayne, and he was Rebekah Heald's uncle.

levels.8-10: William Wells was born in Kentucky. When he was a boy, the Miami people took him. They raised him as one of their own. He married a daughter of Little Turtle, their great war chief. He had fought on both sides in the Indian wars. He worked with the Indians for the government at Fort Wayne. He was Rebekah Heald's uncle.

entries.text: In August 1812 he rode to Chicago with a band of Miami warriors to bring the garrison safely to Fort Wayne, arriving on the 13th. On the 15th he led the column out with his face painted black. He was killed in the fight, and his heart was eaten by warriors who wanted his courage.

levels.8-10: In August 1812 he rode to Chicago with a band of Miami warriors. He came to lead the soldiers safely to Fort Wayne. He got there on the 13th. On the 15th he led the soldiers out with his face painted black. He was killed in the fight. The warriors honored how brave he was.

entries.text: Winnemeg, the Catfish, was a Potawatomi chief of the St. Joseph River, a friend of the Americans who in 1810 kept his people out of Tecumseh's confederacy.

levels.8-10: Winnemeg was a Potawatomi chief of the St. Joseph River. His name means the Catfish. He was a friend of the Americans. In 1810 he kept his people from joining Tecumseh's side.
levels.11-13: Winnemeg, the Catfish, was a Potawatomi chief of the St. Joseph River. He was a friend of the Americans, and in 1810 he kept his people out of Tecumseh's alliance.

entries.text: In August 1812 he carried General Hull's letter ordering the fort evacuated, and urged Heald through Kinzie to go at once. On 15 August, Wau-Bun heard, he and Waubansee tried to save the wounded Wells.

levels.8-10: In August 1812 he carried General Hull's letter. It told the soldiers to leave the fort. Through Kinzie, he told Heald to go right away. The book Wau-Bun says that on 15 August he and Waubansee tried to save Wells, who was hurt.
levels.11-13: In August 1812 he carried General Hull's letter ordering the soldiers to leave the fort. Through Kinzie, he urged Heald to go at once. On 15 August, Wau-Bun heard, he and Waubansee tried to save the wounded Wells.

entries.text: Every few summers I go west to the Rock River to trade with the Sauk. They have horses from the far plains and lead from the mines near the Mississippi, and we have goods from the traders here at the lake. One of their war leaders there is a hard man called Black Hawk, who hates the Americans almost as much as Main Poc does.

levels.8-10: Every few summers I go west to the Rock River to trade with the Sauk. They have horses from the far plains. They have lead from the mines near the Mississippi. We have goods from the traders here at the lake. One of their war leaders is a hard man called Black Hawk. He hates the Americans almost as much as Main Poc does.

entries.text: He told me the Americans took the Sauk land along the Mississippi with a treaty that his people never agreed to, signed by men who were drunk and had no right. He says he will never forgive it. I believe him. I have never met a man who held a grudge so carefully, like a coal kept alive in a shell. One day, I think, that coal will set the prairie burning.

levels.8-10: He told me the Americans took the Sauk land by the Mississippi with a treaty. His people never said yes to it. The men who signed it were drunk and had no right to sign. He says he will never forgive it. I believe him. I have never met a man who kept a grudge so carefully. He keeps it like a hot coal kept alive in a shell. One day, I think, that coal will set the prairie on fire.

entries.text: I came down from Milwaukee three days ago with a party of twenty, along the lake shore trail. At every creek we met others going the same way, from the north and the west, families with their horses and dogs and kettles, all walking toward Chicago.

levels.8-10: I came down from Milwaukee three days ago. Twenty of us walked the trail along the lake shore. At every creek we met others going the same way. They came from the north and the west. Whole families walked with their horses and dogs and kettles. Everyone was walking to Chicago.

entries.text: It was like the whole country was moving, like birds before a storm. Nobody had told us to come. We came because everybody was coming. That is how great things happen, I think. Not because a chief says so. Because everybody starts walking in the same direction at once and nobody can stop.

levels.8-10: It was as if the whole land was moving, like birds before a storm. Nobody told us to come. We came because everybody was coming. I think that is how big things happen. A chief does not say so. Everybody just starts walking the same way at once, and nobody can stop.

entries.text: Everyone in this camp knows the name of Wells. When the Americans' armies came into our country twenty years ago, Wells was scouting for them. He knew where our villages were, and how we fought, because he had been one of the Miami himself. Many of our people died because of what he knew.

levels.8-10: Everyone in this camp knows the name Wells. Twenty years ago the Americans' armies came into our land. Wells was a scout for them. He knew where our villages were and how we fought. He knew because he had been one of the Miami himself. Many of our people died because of what he knew.

entries.text: So when he rode in yesterday with his Miami, some of the young men spat on the ground. Some of the older men nodded to him, because they remember him from before, when he was Little Turtle's son-in-law and the Americans' enemy. A man with two lives has two kinds of enemies. Wells has more than anyone.

levels.8-10: So when he rode in yesterday with his Miami, some of the young men spat on the ground. Some of the older men nodded to him. They remember him from before. Back then he was married to Little Turtle's daughter, and he fought against the Americans. A man with two lives has two kinds of enemies. Wells has more than anyone.

entries.text: Before the traders brought ribbon, my grandmother decorated everything with porcupine quills. You soften them in your mouth, flatten them with your teeth, dye them with roots and berries, and sew them down in patterns so fine you would think they were painted.

levels.8-10: Before the traders brought ribbon, my grandma made everything pretty with porcupine quills. You make them soft in your mouth. You flatten them with your teeth. You dye them with roots and berries. Then you sew them down in patterns so fine you would think they were painted.

entries.text: I still do quillwork on moccasins for my family, though it takes ten times as long as ribbon. My daughter says why bother, when the trader has ribbon in every colour. I tell her: because your grandmother's hands taught mine, and mine will teach yours, and when you sew quills you are holding her hands. She rolls her eyes. One day she will understand.

levels.8-10: I still sew quills on moccasins for my family. It takes ten times as long as ribbon. My daughter says, why bother? The trader has ribbon in every color. I tell her this. Your grandma's hands taught mine, and mine will teach yours. When you sew quills, you are holding her hands. She rolls her eyes. One day she will understand.

entries.text: Last autumn I went south with the young men to the Prophet's town on the Wabash. The Prophet, Tecumseh's brother, said we must give up the white men's goods and their whiskey and live as our grandfathers did, and that if we were strong the Americans would go back over the mountains.

levels.8-10: Last fall I went south with the young men to the Prophet's town on the Wabash River. The Prophet was Tecumseh's brother. He said we must give up the white men's goods and their whiskey. He said we must live like our grandfathers did. If we were strong, he said, the Americans would go back over the mountains.

entries.text: Before dawn on a cold day in November we attacked the army that General Harrison had brought up to the town. I will not tell you about the fighting. When the sun came up we had lost, and the Americans burned the town. The Prophet's medicine had not stopped their bullets. Some men stopped believing in him that day. Some men only started hating the Americans more. I was one of the second.

levels.8-10: Before dawn on a cold day in November, we attacked the army General Harrison had brought to the town. I will not tell you about the fighting. When the sun came up, we had lost. The Americans burned the town. The Prophet's magic had not stopped their bullets. Some men stopped believing in him that day. Some men only hated the Americans more. I was one of those.

entries.text: Every summer the British at Amherstburg, down the river from Detroit, give presents to every nation that comes: blankets, kettles, guns, powder, silver, ribbons, vermilion. They call us their children and the king our father, and they feast us for days.

levels.8-10: Every summer the British at Amherstburg give presents to every nation that comes. Amherstburg is down the river from Detroit. They give blankets, kettles, guns, powder, silver, ribbons and red paint. They call us their children and call the king our father. They feast us for days.

entries.text: The Americans give presents too, at their treaties, but it is never the same. The Americans want land. The British, so far, want only friends. I am not a fool. I know the British want something too. But when a man must choose between a friend who wants nothing yet and a neighbour who wants everything, he chooses the friend. Ask Fox Running what the British promised. He has just come from them.

levels.8-10: The Americans give presents too, at their treaties. But it is never the same. The Americans want land. So far, the British only want friends. I am not a fool. I know the British want something too. But think about it. One is a friend who wants nothing yet. One is a neighbor who wants everything. A man picks the friend. Ask Fox Running what the British promised. He just came from them.

entries.text: In April, when word came of the killings at Lee's farm, every family in the settlement left their houses in the dark. Nobody took anything but the children and a blanket. I carried my youngest on my hip and dragged the other by the hand, and the soldiers held the gate open with lanterns until the last of us was in.

levels.8-10: In April we heard about the killings at Lee's farm. Every family in the town left home in the dark. Nobody took anything but the children and a blanket. I carried my youngest on my hip and pulled the other by the hand. The soldiers held the gate open with lanterns until the last of us was in.

entries.text: We have lived in the fort ever since. Four months, crowded into the officers' quarters and the storerooms with the soldiers' wives. My own house is just over there, a few hundred yards, with the door shut and the garden gone to weeds. I can see it from the walls. I will not see it again after tomorrow.

levels.8-10: We have lived in the fort ever since. That is four months, all crowded into the officers' rooms and storerooms with the soldiers' wives. My own house is just over there, a short walk away. The door is shut, and the garden is full of weeds. I can see it from the walls. After tomorrow I will never see it again.

entries.text: The Kinzies will not march in the column tomorrow. Mrs. Kinzie and the children will go by water, in their own boat, with the boatmen and the nurse, and meet us down the lake. Mr. Kinzie will walk with the soldiers, because he says he will not be seen to hide.

levels.8-10: The Kinzies will not march with the soldiers tomorrow. Mrs. Kinzie and the children will go by water, in their own boat. The boatmen and the nurse will go too. They will meet us down the lake. Mr. Kinzie will walk with the soldiers. He says he will not be seen to hide.

entries.text: Mrs. Kinzie was taken herself as a girl, they say, carried off from Pennsylvania by the Senecas and raised among them, and she knows the people in the camps better than any officer here. She has said nothing about tomorrow, only gone on packing in that quiet way of hers. Find her and ask her. She will tell you more with one look than the captain tells in a speech.

levels.8-10: People say Mrs. Kinzie was taken when she was a girl. The Senecas took her from Pennsylvania and raised her. She knows the people in the camps better than any officer here. She has said nothing about tomorrow. She just keeps packing in her quiet way. Find her and ask her. One look from her tells you more than a speech from the captain.

entries.text: Margaret Helm is seventeen and she married the lieutenant last year, and she is the merriest creature in this whole sad fort. She is Mrs. Kinzie's daughter by her first husband, a British officer, so her late father wore the King's coat and her husband wears the President's.

levels.8-10: Margaret Helm is seventeen. She married the lieutenant last year. She is the most cheerful person in this whole sad fort. Her mom is Mrs. Kinzie. Her real dad was a British officer. So her dad wore the King's coat, and her husband wears the President's.

entries.text: She can ride, and she can shoot, and she has told us all she is not afraid of anything. I think it is mostly true. She is going to ride with the column tomorrow instead of going in her mother's boat, because she will not leave her husband. Find her, and ask her why. She will laugh and tell you, as if it were the simplest thing in the world.

levels.8-10: She can ride, and she can shoot. She has told us all she is not afraid of anything. I think that is mostly true. Tomorrow she will ride with the soldiers instead of going in her mom's boat. She will not leave her husband. Find her and ask her why. She will laugh and tell you, as if it were the easiest thing in the world.

entries.text: Rebekah Heald came here in 1811 on horseback, all the way from Louisville, a bride of twenty, with her husband and her servant Cicely and Cicely's baby. She rode the whole way. The officers' wives in Detroit, they say, would have gone by boat and been carried ashore.

levels.8-10: Rebekah Heald came here in 1811 on horseback, all the way from Louisville. She was a bride of twenty. Her husband came, and so did Cicely, who worked for her, and Cicely's baby. She rode the whole way. People say the officers' wives in Detroit would have gone by boat and been carried to shore.

entries.text: She is the niece of Captain Wells, the scout, and she rides like him, low on the horse's neck, fast. The officers say she is a fine shot as well. Tomorrow she rides with the column. I have seen her checking her saddle girth twice an hour all afternoon. She is not as calm as she looks.

levels.8-10: Her uncle is Captain Wells, the scout. She rides like him, low on the horse's neck, and fast. The officers say she is a good shot too. Tomorrow she rides with the soldiers. All afternoon I have seen her check the strap on her saddle twice an hour. She is not as calm as she looks.

entries.text: Mr. Kinzie was a silversmith before he was a trader, and he still makes the silver himself: brooches, ear-bobs, arm bands, crosses, little round gorgets with holes for the thread. The Potawatomi wear it sewn on their clothes in rows, so that a man in his best coat shines like a lake in the sun.

levels.8-10: Mr. Kinzie made things out of silver before he was a trader. He still makes the silver himself. He makes pins, earrings, arm bands, crosses, and little round pieces with holes for the thread. The Potawatomi sew it on their clothes in rows. A man in his best coat shines like a lake in the sun.

entries.text: That is how Kinzie built the trade here. Not with guns or whiskey, though he sells those too, but with silver that people wanted to wear. He knows every chief's name and every chief's wife's name, and the names of their children. If you want to understand Chicago, find him. He is the town, more than the fort is.

levels.8-10: That is how Kinzie built his trade here. He did it with silver that people wanted to wear, not with guns or whiskey, though he sells those too. He knows every chief's name. He knows every chief's wife's name, and their kids' names too. If you want to understand Chicago, find him. He is the town, more than the fort is.

entries.text: Two months ago, at sunset on the seventeenth of June, Mr. Kinzie and the government interpreter, Jean Lalime, met just outside the gate as it was being shut. Words were said. Nobody agrees what they were about. Some say the trade, some say an old grudge, some say Lalime had been writing letters to Fort Wayne about Kinzie.

levels.8-10: Two months ago, at sunset on 17 June, the gate was being shut. Mr. Kinzie and Jean Lalime met just outside it. Lalime turned Indian words into English for the army. The two men said angry words. Nobody agrees what it was about. Some say the trade. Some say an old fight. Some say Lalime had been writing letters to Fort Wayne about Kinzie.

entries.text: They fought, and when it was over Kinzie had a wound in his neck and Lalime lay dead. A friend took Kinzie off to Milwaukee that night, until it was safe to come back. Lalime is buried in front of the Kinzie house, inside a little picket fence, where Kinzie sees the grave every morning from his porch. I do not know how a man drinks his coffee looking at that.

levels.8-10: They fought. When it was over, Kinzie was cut on the neck, and Lalime was dead. A friend took Kinzie to Milwaukee that night, until it was safe to come back. Lalime is buried in front of the Kinzie house, inside a little fence. Kinzie sees the grave from his porch every morning. I do not know how a man can drink his coffee looking at that.

entries.text: Across from the fort stands the government's trading house, the factory. The idea was that the government would sell goods to the Potawatomi at a fair price, cheaper than the British traders, and so win their friendship. Mr. Irwin, the factor, ran it for three years, and in all that time he complained that the Indians liked Kinzie's goods better than his.

levels.8-10: Across from the fort stands the government's store, called the factory. The plan was for the government to sell goods to the Potawatomi at a fair price. It would be cheaper than the British traders. That would make them friends. Mr. Irwin ran it for three years. The whole time, he grumbled that the Indians liked Kinzie's goods better.

entries.text: He left in July and gave the keys to Doctor Van Voorhis. Now the store is being emptied out to the camps, as the captain promised, bolts of cloth, kettles, blankets, paint. The people take them and look at the fort and do not say thank you. You cannot buy a friend in a week with what you would not sell him for three years.

levels.8-10: He left in July and gave the keys to Doctor Van Voorhis. Now the store is being emptied out to the camps, as the captain promised. Out go cloth, kettles, blankets and paint. The people take them and look at the fort. They do not say thank you. You cannot buy a friend in a week with things you would not sell him for three years.

entries.text: Jean Baptiste Chandonnai is Mr. Kinzie's clerk, and he is the only man in Chicago who is welcome in every house and every lodge. He is French and Potawatomi both, and young, and he moves between the trading house and the camps like a fish between rocks.

levels.8-10: Jean Baptiste Chandonnai is Mr. Kinzie's clerk. He is the only man in Chicago who is welcome in every house and every lodge. He is French and Potawatomi both, and he is young. He slips between the trading house and the camps like a fish between rocks.

entries.text: He keeps the books, and he translates, and he carries messages. This week he has been carrying a great many messages. Everyone wants to know what everyone else is thinking, and he is the only one who can ask. If you find him, he will greet you kindly. He is very good at greeting people kindly and telling them nothing.

levels.8-10: He keeps the books. He turns words from one language to another. He carries messages. This week he has carried lots of messages. Everyone wants to know what everyone else is thinking, and he is the only one who can ask. If you find him, he will greet you kindly. He is very good at greeting people kindly and telling them nothing.

entries.text: Last winter I was sent with the goods to a wintering post on the Kankakee River, two of us and a Potawatomi family who traded with us. For four months I saw no other white face. The snow came up to the roof of our hut and the wolves sat in a ring around it at night and sang.

levels.8-10: Last winter I was sent with the goods to a trading post on the Kankakee River for the winter. There were two of us, and a Potawatomi family who traded with us. For four months I saw no other white face. The snow came up to the roof of our hut. At night the wolves sat in a ring around it and howled.

entries.text: The family took us in when our flour ran out. The old woman gave me a pair of moccasins lined with rabbit fur, and I wore them until they fell to pieces. When I came back to Chicago in the spring I had forgotten how to talk to Americans. I have not entirely remembered.

levels.8-10: When our flour ran out, the family took us in. The old woman gave me moccasins lined with rabbit fur. I wore them until they fell apart. When I came back to Chicago in the spring, I had forgotten how to talk to Americans. I still have not quite remembered.

entries.text: Mr. Kinzie keeps a lodging house beside his own for us, his hired men. Bunks, a fire, a table, a fiddle on the wall that nobody can play properly. In the evening we sit there and smoke and argue about which of us has the worst back.

levels.8-10: Mr. Kinzie keeps a house next to his own for us, his hired men. It has bunks, a fire, a table, and a fiddle on the wall that nobody can play well. In the evening we sit there and smoke. We argue about which of us has the worst back.

entries.text: Tonight nobody is arguing. Everybody is mending something, or sharpening something, or packing something. Old Baptiste, who is the best storyteller among us, started a story about a werewolf in Quebec and stopped halfway through, and nobody asked him to finish. That never happens.

levels.8-10: Tonight nobody is arguing. Everybody is fixing something, or sharpening something, or packing something. Old Baptiste tells the best stories of all of us. He started a story about a werewolf in Quebec. He stopped halfway, and nobody asked him to finish. That never happens.

entries.text: Listen at dawn tomorrow and you will hear George Burnett's fife before you hear the birds. He has been on the rolls since 1806 and he can play every call the army ever wrote, and a few it never did. He plays reveille as if he is angry at the sun for being late.

levels.8-10: Listen at dawn tomorrow. You will hear George Burnett's fife before you hear the birds. A fife is a little flute. He has been a soldier since 1806. He can play every tune the army ever wrote, and a few it never did. He plays the wake-up call as if he is mad at the sun for being late.

entries.text: In the winter, when the snow comes up to the pickets and there is nothing to do but mend boots, he plays jigs in the barracks and the men dance with each other because there is nobody else to dance with. I have seen a sergeant waltz a corporal round the stove. If you want to hear him, ask nicely. He pretends to be shy and then plays until you beg him to stop.

levels.8-10: In the winter, the snow piles up to the fence, and there is nothing to do but fix boots. Then he plays dance tunes in the barracks. The men dance with each other, since there is nobody else to dance with. I once saw a sergeant waltz a corporal around the stove. If you want to hear him, ask nicely. He acts shy. Then he plays until you beg him to stop.

entries.text: I enlisted at seventeen because a recruiting sergeant in Pennsylvania bought me supper and told me about the West. He did not mention the mosquitoes. He did not mention the fevers, or the winters, or the way the wind comes off the lake in January and goes straight through a wool coat as if it were paper.

levels.8-10: I joined the army at seventeen. A sergeant in Pennsylvania bought me supper and told me about the West. He did not say a word about the mosquitoes. He did not talk about the fevers, or the winters. He did not tell me how the January wind off the lake goes right through a wool coat like paper.

entries.text: But he did not lie about the West. I have seen buffalo on the far prairie, a dark smudge moving like a cloud shadow. I have seen the lake turn green and gold and grey in a single afternoon. If I get home I will tell my brothers about it, and they will not believe a word.

I have seen the lake turn green, then gold, then gray, all in one afternoon. If I get home, I will tell my brothers about it. They will not believe a word.

entries.text: After the killings in April, the captain made soldiers of every grown man in the settlement who was not already one. Twelve of us. Thomas Burns is our sergeant, an old soldier himself who stayed on here when his time was up and married a widow with a houseful of children.

levels.8-10: After the killings in April, the captain made soldiers of every grown man in town who was not one already. There are twelve of us. Thomas Burns is our sergeant. He was a soldier himself. When his time was up, he stayed here and married a widow with a house full of kids.

entries.text: We drill on the parade with the regulars, and they laugh at us, because we march like farmers going to market, which is what we are. But every one of us has a family inside these walls. A man fights differently when the wagon behind him holds his own children. Find Burns. He will tell you we are getting better. That is very nearly true.

entries.text: I came here from Detroit as second in command and married the trader's stepdaughter, and some of the officers have not forgiven me for being happy. Margaret is the bravest girl in the Northwest. She has told me she will ride beside the column tomorrow, and I have stopped arguing.

entries.text: I disagreed with the captain about the march. I said so once, properly, and then I held my tongue, because that is what an officer does. entries.card: why:ADOPTED FROM THE CURREY BIRD'S-EYE, BY OWNER RULING. The 1912 plate draws a small building in the fort's north-east inner angle under an unmistakable four-sided cap: a point apex, two hips running down to the eave corners and no ridge. Only the roof clears the picket row in that view, so the cap is the one thing of this building the drawing shows. The owner compared the plate with Whistler's 1808 draught building by building and chose to take the pyramid here while keeping Whistler's measured plan for everything else. WHAT THE DRAWING SUPPLIES IS THE SHAPE AND NOTHING ELSE. It is retrospective - Currey 1912, after a Chicago Daily Tribune sketch of 1899 of Van den Berghen's 1898 model - and not to scale: its own camera here is diagnostic only, and the same fit cannot hold both the plan corners and the flagstaff. So the pitch below stays 34 degrees reconstructed, the footprint stays the register's half-measured 12.2 x 10.0 ft and the wall stays 2.4 m; none of the three is read off the plate. Whistler's draught is cited beside it because the building, its place and its front are his (index no. 16, drawn in elevation) and the sheet is silent on the roof - this attribute is inferred from the later picture standing on the contemporary identification, and it was 'gable', reconstructed and unattested, before the owner ruled. the liberties register records what the shape still leaves invented.

levels.8-10: We took this roof from a picture by Currey. The owner of this project chose it. The picture, from 1912, shows a small building in the fort's north-east corner. Its roof comes to a point, with four sides. Only the roof shows over the fence in that picture, so the roof is all it tells us. The owner looked at the picture and an old map from 1808, building by building. The owner took the pointed roof from the picture and kept the map for all the rest. The picture was made long after the fort was gone, from an old model. It is not drawn to size. So the slope of the roof, the size of the building and the height of the walls are our guesses. None of them is read off the picture. The 1808 map shows the building and where it stood, but not its roof. Before the owner chose, the roof was a plain two-sided one, and that was a guess too.

entries.card: why:Fractions of the ridge from its EAST end, which is the footprint frame's -x end at this record's 180-degree facing. Nobody is placed in it (“No people, anywhere”).

levels.8-10: The old map calls this the Interpreter's House. It was the home of the man who spoke for the fort with the Native people. It stood west of the fort. levels.8-10: We measured this garden with the old map's own scale, 50 feet to an inch. That reading of the scale is our guess. Its four sides make a box 229 by 115 feet. The map's lines were drawn by hand, so the box is our guess too.

entries.card: why:Moses and Kirkland vol.1p.30 (committed text lines4953–4955): 'The house was of squared logs, after the fashion of the very best of the frontier mansions of that day.' This attests the substrate, not an uncoated dark finish. Other work retains the squared-log fabric and states its whitewash separately as a reconstructed choice; no weatherboard cladding or installation date is invented.

levels.8-10: A book by Moses and Kirkland says: 'The house was of squared logs, after the fashion of the very best of the frontier mansions of that day.' That tells us the logs. It does not say they were left dark. We kept the squared logs. Painting them white is our own choice. We did not add boards on the outside, and we did not make up a date for any.

entries.card: why:NO SOURCE PLACES THE MIAMIS' CAMP; THIS GROUND IS OURS. Heald, Helm and Currey say only that Wells came from Fort Wayne with about thirty Miamis 'mounted on ponies' (Currey 1912) and that they marched out on the 15th, part before the column and part behind it (Heald's report, Quaife 1913 Appendix IV). Mounted men come to march the garrison out would camp by the fort, by its stables and the road south they would take, and apart from the Potawatomi gathering on the creek; so the ground stands on the level prairie about 40 m south of the fort's three stables and 175 m south-west of the outer pickets (the owner, 2026-11-08: build the camps 'where they would most logically have been'): local E +1060..+1090, N +56..+80. Its outline lies between -0.01 and +0.04 m of the origin's 2.49 m on the the 1830 natural ground heightfield; it keeps 15 m from every 1812 footprint, 6 m from every worn trail and 4 m from the wagon roads of other work (the fort's south loop and the shore road). The point recorded is the ground's south-west corner. “Lodges for the whole August 1812 gathering: seven more grounds on the creek, the occupancy rule, and a camp for Wells's Miami escort”.

levels.8-10: No paper says where the Miami men camped. We chose this ground. Old accounts say only that Wells came from Fort Wayne with about thirty Miami men on ponies. On the 15th they marched out, some in front of the soldiers and some behind. Men on horses, come to lead the soldiers out, would camp near the fort. They would be near its stables and the road south. They would be apart from the Potawatomi camp by the creek. So we put the camp on flat prairie, about 40 meters south of the fort's stables. The owner of this project asked for the camps to go where they most likely were. The ground here is flat. The camp keeps clear of every building, path and road.

entries.card: why:No occupied upper storey or dormer is established by the credited pictures. Sarony's small gable light is modelled explicitly under end openings; it is not evidence of an occupied loft. The earlier note saying no picture drew a gable opening was superseded when other work adopted that light.

levels.8-10: No old picture shows people living up under the roof, or a window on the roof. One picture by Sarony shows a small window at the end of the roof, and we built it. It does not mean anyone lived up there. An old note said no picture showed such a window. That note was wrong, and we fixed it.

entries.card: why:No source states what this house was built of. Log is the bounded reading: every house the histories describe at the post before 1812 whose material they give is log (the Kinzie house, the agency house, the factory, Lee's Place, the cabin Hurlbut judged to be this one), and the piece of work's own inventory builds the settlement at the log dwelling archetype. Recorded as a liberty (“The Burns and Lee houses of 1812: their seats, sizes, fabric and closing dates”).

levels.8-10: No paper says what this house was built of. We say logs. Every house at the fort before 1812 that the old books describe was made of logs. That includes the Kinzie house, the agent's house, the trading house, Lee's Place and the cabin Hurlbut thought was this one. So we built it of logs. That is our guess, and we wrote it down.

entries.card: why:Not stated; timber like the rest of the post. Boarded rather than log (at the first bake): at 1.7 x 2.4 m a notched log pen's corners would meet near the middle of its walls, so a house this small is the post's boarded kind, and timber is all Quaife's reading gives either way.

levels.8-10: No paper says what it was made of. We built it of wood like the rest of the fort. We used boards, not logs. It is so small that log corners would almost meet in the middle of the walls. A book by Quaife says only that it was wood.

entries.card: why:OPENS ON THE DRAUGHT'S DATE, CLOSES WITH THE DECADE THE EXCLUSION GIVES IT. It opens on 25 January 1808, the date in the parade of Whistler's draught, the first day a source draws this house; Ouilmette had lived at Chicago since 1790 by Currey's account and Mrs. Whistler counted his among the four huts of 1803 (Moses and Kirkland v1 p. 35), so it may well be older. It STANDS IN AUGUST 1812 BY THE SOURCES, not by continuity: Wau-Bun ch. XIX has Mrs. Helm hidden in it on the 16th and a sergeant climb in at its back window the next afternoon, and Currey (1912) has the family alone of the village's residents not leave their dwelling. Hubbard, listing every building in the present limits of Cook County when he came in 1818, still has 'a cabin on the north side occupied by Antoine Ouilmette' (his autobiography, the inventory of 1818). It closes on 31 December 1829, which is the exclusions record Antoine Ouilmette's cabin's own bound: Ouilmette left for Gross Pointe in the later 1820s and no source attests the cabin past that decade. Out of 1835. “Antoine Ouilmette's house of 1812: the drawn house taken as his, its height and pitch, its closing date, and the currant bushes behind it”.

levels.8-10: It first shows on 25 January 1808, the date on an old map of the fort by Whistler. That is the first time anyone draws this house. It may be older. One account says Ouilmette lived at Chicago from 1790. Mrs. Whistler counted his house as one of four huts in 1803. Old books say it still stood in August 1812. The book Wau-Bun says Mrs. Helm hid in it on the 16th. The next day a soldier climbed in at its back window. Currey says this family was the only one in the village that did not leave home. Hubbard came in 1818. He listed every building in the area, and he still lists Ouilmette's cabin north of the river. We end the cabin on 31 December 1829. Ouilmette moved away to Gross Pointe in the late 1820s. No paper shows the cabin after that. So it is not in the 1835 town.

levels.8-10: One chimney. A picture from 1912 draws it outside one end of the house. It is the left end, seen from the river, at the front corner.

entries.card: why:Other work picture refinement. Kurz & Allison (1893), panel 1, draws each first-fort blockhouse with a roof lantern and no separate chimney. The former one-stack value was an unattested heating reconstruction; removing that invented stack follows the pictured silhouette without asserting that a retrospective print proves historical absence. The lantern itself and the panel's conflicting tower locations remain unresolved; no plan, bearing or documented 75 ft flagstaff is changed. The complete 1812 total (including possible hidden fittings or schematic omissions) remains reconstructed; this is a conservative model choice to follow visible evidence, not positive proof of the historical total or absence. Source-visible counts remain explicit.

levels.8-10: A picture from 1893 by Kurz and Allison draws each of the fort's two towers with a small lookout on the roof and no chimney. We had built one chimney, but that was only our guess. We took it away to match the picture. The picture was made long after, so it does not prove there was no chimney. The lookout, and where the picture puts the towers, are still not sure. We did not move anything else. The full count of chimneys in 1812 is still our guess.

entries.card: why:Other work upper gallery refinement. Whistler’s 1808 index attests two-storey barracks with 'Galliaries fronting the parade', without counting gallery levels. Currey’s 1912 retrospective bird’s-eye shows a covered upper walk with a vertical-pale railing over an open lower gallery on the visible courtyard ranges. Two levels are inferred for this member of the same garrison ranges, not claimed as a separately identified contemporary elevation of this individual facade. Gallery reach, post and floor sections, railing height and spacing, and roof fall are reconstructed; the 1808 folded elevations are not used as height scales. No surveyed placement or range footprint changes. Follow-up support placement: where explicit front rectangles exist, retain the old support count/rhythm but project a colliding post centre to the nearest solid pier clearing both storeys' rectangles and the existing casing/sill-horn envelope. This algorithm/placement and all sections remain reconstructed. Rail density/height and remaining occlusion are unresolved; no upper entrance or accessible gallery interior is asserted.

levels.8-10: An old map from 1808 says the soldiers' houses were two floors high, with porches facing the yard. It does not say how many porch floors there were. A picture by Currey from 1912 shows a covered walk up top, with a rail, over an open porch below. So we built two porch floors here too. That is our guess for this building. How deep the porch is, its posts, floors, rail and roof are our guesses too. Where a post would hit a window, we moved it to the nearest solid wall. Nothing else moved. We do not say there was a door to the top porch.

entries.card: why:Other work visible completion: the household's Sarony plate draws the front pale and its gable light in shade; Currey's caption expressly covers1804–1813 as well as1816–1828. Eastman's1820 plate also draws the main house's gable light. These do not date a coating to August1812, so using the existing whitewash finish on both squared logs and chinking is reconstructed continuity, not an attested paint colour/date or an assertion of weatherboards. It replaces the previous unsupported assumption that every pale depiction necessarily showed a later cladding. The hewn-log relief remains. “The Kinzie house's whitewashed logs, taller end door and bounded green” records the choice.

levels.8-10: An old picture by Sarony shows the front fence and the window at the end of the roof in light colors. Currey says his picture covers 1804 to 1813 and 1816 to 1828. A picture by Eastman from 1820 also shows that end window. None of these says the house was painted white in August 1812. We painted the logs white, but that is our guess. We do not say it had boards on the outside. We used to think every light picture meant boards were added later. That was only a guess, and we took it out. The cut logs still show.

A2.50m clear opening, with its0.02m sill, follows that relative head line and corrects a greater-than0.3m visible miss. It is bounded by the retained3.0m wall, not a measured historical height. levels.8-10: In Sarony's picture, the door at the west end is taller than our first door. Its top was about level with the window next to it. So we made the door 2.5 meters tall, with a low step. That matches the picture better. The wall is 3 meters tall, so the door cannot be taller than that. Its height is our guess, not a measure. The door's width and place, the front door and the other windows did not change.

entries.card: why:Other work, the owner's reading of Currey's bird's-eye (2026-11-07): each face of the cupola's cap carries a small dark opening, a lookout to see far off. The drawing shows two faces of each cap with one opening apiece; the other two faces are taken to match. It is too small to give the openings' shape or size, so each is built as a small framed opening under a shed hood, its width, height and place on the face reconstructed (fort structure params cupola port_*; the liberties register “cupolas on the first fort's two blockhouses”).
