levels.8-10: The owner of this project looked at a picture by Currey. Each side of the tower's little roof has a small dark hole, to look out far. The picture shows two sides of each roof with one hole each. We gave the other two sides one each too. The picture is too small to show their shape or size. So we built each as a small framed hole under a little roof. Their size and place are our guesses.

entries.card: why:Other work, the owner's reading of the pictures (2026-11-07): the cupola is laid in log like the rest of the blockhouse, not boarded. Currey's bird's-eye draws the cupola bodies with the same horizontal courses as the walls below them, and a garrison building its blockhouses in log would raise the lookout on top the same way. Course height, notching and chinking are the blockhouse's own (coursed log wall, “The first Fort Dearborn's heights, roofs, stacks, pickets and two missing depths are ours”); nothing in the pictures measures them.

levels.8-10: The owner of this project looked at the pictures. The lookout on top of the tower is made of logs, like the rest of the tower, not boards. Currey's picture draws it with the same rows as the walls below. Men building the towers of logs would build the lookout the same way. How thick the logs are and how they meet are our own, like the rest of the tower. The pictures do not measure them.

entries.card: why:Owner adoption: Currey's 1912 retrospective bird's-eye labels the magazine (8) under a rounded vault, consistent with Whistler's 1808 arched front. Adopt that roof shape for the first-fort 1812 phase only. These sources give no vault radius, rise, thickness, colour or construction date. The contemporary surveyed seat, bearing and front width remain unchanged; neither the retrospective picture nor its diagnostic camera supplies a metric fit.

levels.8-10: The owner of this project chose this roof. A picture by Currey from 1912 shows the gunpowder hut with a round roof. That fits an old map from 1808, which draws an arched front. We use that roof shape for the first fort in 1812 only. The pictures do not say how big the curve is, how thick, what color, or when it was built. Where the hut stands, which way it faces and how wide it is did not change. The pictures do not measure it.

entries.card: why:PLACED BEHIND THE WEST END, AS THREE PICTURES DRAW IT, NOT MEASURED. Sarony, the Cram plate and the Teich painting, all from across the river to the south-west, draw a low building with a stack immediately behind the house's west gable, its west end standing a little beyond the gable's line. Cast through the house's solved cameras at this depth, the west end's back eave corner falls 0.0 m (Sarony), 1.2 m (Cram) and 2.7 m (Teich) west of the house's west wall line, and it is set at their mean, 1.3 m; its depth behind the house no picture can give, and it is set just clear of the house's back eave; the west cottonwood (kinzie house 1812 trees), whose place is that record's own, was moved 3.5 m north to stand clear of it (the liberties register “The Kinzie establishment of 1812: which pictured building is which, where the unpictured ones stand, their sizes, and the rulings on du Sable's bill of sale”).

levels.8-10: We placed this behind the west end of the house, the way three pictures draw it. We did not measure it. Three pictures, all made from across the river, show a low building with a chimney just behind the west end. Its far end sticks out a little past the house. Working from the pictures, its corner falls 0 to 3 meters west of the house. We set it in the middle, about 1.3 meters. The pictures cannot show how far back it is. So we set it just clear of the back of the house. We moved a tree 3.5 meters north to make room. Which building is which in the pictures, and where the rest stand, are our guesses.

entries.card: why:PLACED BY THIS RECORD, IN THE SHADE BEHIND THE HOUSE. Wau-Bun says only that the buildings surrounded the dwelling. No picture draws a dairy: from across the river the house and its cottonwoods hide this spot, and Eastman's view of 1820 does not reach it. A dairy wants shade and the kitchen door, so it stands between the two great cottonwoods, close behind the house (the liberties register “The Kinzie establishment of 1812: which pictured building is which, where the unpictured ones stand, their sizes, and the rulings on du Sable's bill of sale”).

levels.8-10: We placed this ourselves, in the shade behind the house. Wau-Bun says only that the buildings stood around the house. No picture shows a milk house. From across the river, the house and its trees hide this spot. A milk house needs shade and should be near the kitchen door. So we put it between the two big trees, just behind the house. That is our guess.

entries.card: why:PLACED BY TWO STATEMENTS AND THE 1812 GROUND, NOT MEASURED. Wau-Bun: 'On the northern bank of the river, directly facing the fort'; Currey: 'near the present foot of Pine Street', facing south 'having the river directly in front'. So the house is centred on the flagstaff's easting (E +1152, the fort's seat in the 1812 scenes data) and set back from the the 1830 natural ground north bank, which stands at about N +305 there and reaches its level 1.5 m ground by N +318, far enough to leave the 'broad green space... inclosed between it and the river' the same sentence gives: 18 m of green between the piazza and the bank top. The set-back is this record's own (the liberties register “The Kinzie house in 1812: its size, its set-back, its piazza's measure, the green's corners and where its trees stand”).

levels.8-10: We placed this from two old accounts and the shape of the ground. We did not measure it. Wau-Bun says the house was on the north bank of the river, right across from the fort. Currey says it was near where Pine Street ends, facing south with the river in front. So the house lines up with the fort's flag pole. It is set back from the river bank. The same book tells of a big green yard between the house and the river. We left 18 meters of green between the porch and the top of the bank. How far back the house sits is our guess.

entries.card: why:PLACED BY other work's NORTH-BANK RULE, NOT MEASURED. The draught lays nothing outside the garrison down to scale, so this is the sheet's ARRANGEMENT opened out: the field's box offset from the Kinzie house's drawn centre (no. 30, px 1335, 501.5), multiplied by the bank's own expansion (about 2.50: the drafter's '52 yards in length' on the picket between two of the no. 31 houses against its drawn length), added to The Kinzie house, built by Jean Baptiste Point du Sable's footprint centre. That rule, not the main gate's, is the one the houses beside it stand by, so the field keeps its drawn place against them. The field's box on the sheet is px [547, 433, 731, 541] about its centre, drawn turned 29.5 degrees anticlockwise. the whistler 1808 reader --check (run by the project's gate) refuses this point if it is not what the rule gives, to 0.01 m, refuses any corner on the committed 1812 water, and refuses the field standing on any of the houses. The sheet's orientation (its right taken as east) is itself inferred, so the turn on the ground is the turn on the paper and no more (“Coursoll's inclosed field north of the river: its place and size by the north-bank rule, one box for a skewed drawing kept off the house at its corner, its east side and its rails”).

entries.card: why:PLACED WHERE TWO PICTURES' LINES OF SIGHT CROSS, NOT MEASURED. Eastman's view of 1820, taken from up the bank to the east-north-east, draws a low gabled log building between the eye and the Kinzie house's east end, horses before it; Sarony's lithograph of Juliette Kinzie's sketch, taken from across the river to the south-west, draws a small gabled building east of the house behind the poplar row, and the Cram plate and the Teich painting draw it in the same place. Cast through the solved cameras of the house (the kinzie house 1812 data), the two lines cross about 21 m east and 14 m north of the house's north-east corner, and the building stands there. The later pictures fix the place only, not the form: the whitewashed building they draw end-on, with a window in its west gable, will not take one heading with Eastman's log stable (no heading shows both as drawn), so it is this building altered by about 1831 or another on its site, and Eastman's view, drawn on the spot in 1820, governs the form. Pictures are a modern reconstruction, form only, so the place is this record's and is graded so (the liberties register “The Kinzie establishment of 1812: which pictured building is which, where the unpictured ones stand, their sizes, and the rulings on du Sable's bill of sale”).

entries.card: why:PLANNED IN 1808 AND PICTURED AFTER; NEVER DATED (owner adoption 2026-11-03). Whistler's 1808 draught lays the cupolas down on both blockhouses and its index says they were 'not yet built... as laid down', so they were intended and not yet standing then. Kurz & Allison (1893) panel 1 draws a small roof lantern on each first-fort blockhouse and no stack, and Currey's 1912 bird's-eye (after the 1899 Tribune sketch of Van den Berghen's 1898 model) draws a small square body under its own pyramid cap on both. Intent plus two later depictions is what carries INFERRED that they were finished before the fort burned in August 1812; no source dates their completion, both pictures are a modern reconstruction retrospectives, and Whistler's note is kept as the counter-evidence for the years before. EVERY DIMENSION IS RECONSTRUCTED and none is in this record: the side, the height, the cap's pitch and eave and the plain boarded sides are the fort structure archetype's cupola kit (the second fort's), reused at the proportions both pictures show, and the liberties register “cupolas on the first fort's two blockhouses” owns them. No louvres, glazing or finial is built.

entries.card: why:SEATED ACROSS THE RIVER FROM THE CABIN, ON other work's RULING, NOT MEASURED. Wau-Bun gives the side and nothing else: the stacks stood 'on the opposite bank' from the cabin, close enough that the soldier, walking down to the canoes, pointed to them across the water and was soon over to them, the stream between 'narrow', with woods 'close at hand' behind them. The cabin's bank is the north-west one by other work's ruling (the 1812 hardscrabble site data, which states the placings it rests on), so the stacks are on the south-east bank. THE RULING HERE: the four stacks stand as a loose group on the line through other work's station and the channel's centre, carried on across the river along the bank's own normal (bearing 147 degrees), between 42 and 62 m from the centre - beyond the bank face other work's apron draws, on its 1.31 m land grade - and up to 14 m up or down the river from that line, with 8 to 12 m of meadow between neighbours, room for cattle to stand among them and for two men to walk round them out of sight of the far bank. Every distance is this project's (“Lee's Place in 1812: four haystacks on the bank opposite the cabin, their count, size, place and season”). If the reach moves, the stacks move with it.

levels.8-10: We placed these hay stacks across the river from the cabin. We did not measure them. Wau-Bun says only that the stacks were on the far bank from the cabin. A soldier walked down to the canoes, pointed to them over the water, and soon got to them. The river there was narrow, with woods close behind. We put the cabin on the north-west bank, so the stacks are on the south-east bank. There are four stacks in a loose group, 42 to 62 meters from the river. entries.card: why:SEATED BY STATED RULE, NOT MEASURED. Whistler draws three houses west of Kinzie's, each with a '31' ('Oather Dwelling Houses on opisite side River'), and says his outside distances are 'not laid down by a scale'. Other work's rule opens the sheet out about the main gate; here it is opened out about the Kinzie house as built (The Kinzie house, built by Jean Baptiste Point du Sable, seated by its texts on the flagstaff's easting), because about the gate it would put the no. 31 houses east of that house when the sheet draws them west of it. The expansion is the drafter's own '52 yards in length', lettered on the picket he draws along this bank between the westernmost house and the middle one: 2.497 times the drawing, where no. 17's eighteen perches would give 3.322 and set the two houses 74 m apart against the fence's 47.5. The house faces south to the river, as the draught draws its front. the whistler 1808 reader --check re-derives this seat from the sheet boxes and refuses it wet or on a neighbour. “La Lime's and Le Mai's houses of 1812: which drawn house is whose, the north bank's frame, their sizes, heights and closing dates”.

entries.card: why:SEATED ON THE COMMITTED RIVER, NOT ON THE SHEET'S. The draught draws no. 27 as a small dotted outline off its river line west of the fort, beside the red '122 feet to River', and says 'The River is not regularly surveyed', so its position on the page is not read. What is kept is the drafter's distance and his side: a circle of 122 ft about the outer picket row's north-west corner, swept from due west, first meets the 1812 water (the river data) 18 degrees north of west, and the deck is centred there and laid along the bank. The rule and its figures are the whistler 1808 fort dearborn data index no. 27 `seat`; the whistler 1808 reader --check (run by the project's gate) recomputes this point, turn, plan and deck height and refuses the record if any has moved. Where it stands is a reconstruction (the liberties register “The first fort's wharf and its covered way to the river stand on the committed 1812 river, by the drafter's one distance and Quaife's one sentence”). IT LAPS THE PLATTED KINZIE STREET BY 5.15 m, AND THAT IS REFUSED IN WRITING, NOT REPAIRED (the corridor intrusion baseline tool `refused`). The corridor is the town's platted street, and no plat of Chicago existed before James Thompson's of 4 August 1830 (Thompson, James. Plat of the Town of Chicago); this record's one phase closes on 16 August 1812. A street eighteen years in the future is not a reason to move a wharf off the river it served, and the only translation that clears the corridor (10.4 m due south, the corridor intrusion check --escape) would stand it on the bank's crest, away from the water.

levels.8-10: We placed this dock on our river, not where the old map draws it. The map draws it as a small dotted shape west of the fort, by the words '122 feet to River'. But the map also says the river was not measured with care. So we kept only his distance and his side. We went 122 feet out from the fort's north-west corner and found where that meets the river. The dock sits there, along the bank. A check makes sure it has not moved. Where it stands is our guess. It lies across where Kinzie Street would be one day. But no town plan was made until 1830, and the dock is gone after 1812. A street from the future is no reason to move the dock away from its river.

entries.card: why:SEATED ON other work's RULING, NOT MEASURED. the 1812 hardscrabble site data rules the farm onto a REACH of the north-west bank, 0.25 to 0.75 mi below Bridgeport by river, with its station half a mile below (Hubbard's 'about half a mile below Bridgeport... on the north side of the river, (south branch)'), at local E -1638.9, N -4249.5; it says the cabin's place on that reach is this piece of work's. THE RULING HERE: the cabin's centre stands 30 m inland of the station along the bank's own normal (bearing 331 degrees), on other work's apron at its 1.31 m land grade, with its long front facing the river (rotation 151 degrees, the normal reversed). Why near the bank: every account puts the cabin by the water - Wau-Bun has the men's canoes 'tied near the bank' in sight of the cabin door, Currey says the farm and the fort talked 'by means of canoes', and the 1912 plate ('Hardscrabble.' Halftone plate facing p. 74 of J. Seymour Currey, The Story of…, a modern reconstruction) draws the house a few rods back from the bank inside the field's fence with a canoe below it. The 30 m is this project's (“Lee's Place in 1812: the cabin's seat, size and shape, the field's bounds and fence, and the closing date”); the plate gives no distance. Why the station's normal and not a point up or down the reach: no source distinguishes one place on the reach from another, so the cabin takes the one point the ruling names. The bearing to the fort is about 3.3 miles in a straight line, inside Heald's 'about three miles from the garrison' ('s own test). If the reach moves, the cabin moves with it.

levels.8-10: We placed this by an earlier choice, not a measure. We put the farm on the north-west bank of the river, a little below Bridgeport. Hubbard says it was about half a mile below Bridgeport, on the north side of the South Branch. The cabin stands 30 meters back from the river, its long front facing the water. Why near the river? Every account puts the cabin by the water. Wau-Bun says the men's canoes were tied near the bank, in sight of the cabin door. Currey says the farm and the fort talked by canoe. A picture from 1912 draws the house a little back from the bank, inside the fence, with a canoe below. The 30 meters is our guess. The picture gives no distance. The cabin is about 3 miles from the fort, and Heald said about three miles. If the river moves, the cabin moves with it.

entries.card: why:SEATED WITH ONE ORIGIN AND ONE BEARING FOR ALL FOURTEEN, so no building moves against another. The box is the register's (the whistler 1808 fort dearborn data), read off the commandant's own measured draught at 4.52 px per foot from the 75 ft staff, good to about +/-1.1 ft an edge. THE ORIGIN: the staff's foot, which the register finds at the centre of the parade and within about a foot of the centre of both picket rows, is set on the fort site at local E +1152, N +221 - the Wright 1834 reading of the fort's place that the project's roadmap S5a cross-checks to 35 m against the modern landmark. That is the SITE, not the second fort's plan: John H. Kinzie (quoted on "Fort Dearborn History." Chicagology) says the first fort 'stood upon the same ground as the last Fort' and 'was differently constructed', so the place carries over and nothing of the 1816 geometry does. THE BEARING: the frame's north is set on grid north, which is the register's own inference that the sheet's right is east, from the lake lettered down that margin; the sheet has no north arrow, so the bearing is inferred and adds nothing to it. The second fort's 8 degrees, read off Harrison 1830, is that fort's and is not borrowed. Grid and true north differ here by under half a degree. A CHECK, NOT A FIT: seated so, the outward row's west side stands about 124 ft from the 1812 river (the river data) and the north-west blockhouse about 65 ft from it; the draught's red-ink '122 feet to River' from the west side and Wilson's '80 feet' from the north-west corner are figures of that size. Carry the datum's +/-20 m on the whole frame.

levels.8-10: All fourteen fort buildings are placed from one point and one direction, so none moves against another. Their sizes come from the fort's own careful plan of 1808, read off it to about a foot. The point is the foot of the flag pole, in the middle of the yard. We set it on the fort's site, read from an old map of 1834. We checked that place against today's landmark, to within 35 meters. That is the site, not the second fort's plan. John H. Kinzie says the first fort stood on the same ground as the last one but was built another way. So we kept the place and nothing of the 1816 fort. The plan has no north arrow. We say its right side is east, since the lake is drawn down that side. That is our guess. The second fort's slant is its own, and we did not borrow it. As a check: our river is about 124 feet from the west side, and the plan says 122 feet. Wilson says 80 feet from the north-west corner, and we have about 65. The whole fort could be off by about 20 meters.

entries.card: why:THE CAMP OF THE AUGUST GATHERING, DATED BY TWO EVENTS AND NOT BY A DAY IT WAS PITCHED. It opens on 12 August 1812: 'The Indians being assembled from the neighboring villages, a council was held with them on the afternoon of the 12th' (Wau-Bun ch. XVIII), so the gathering was camped by then; Heald's letter has them coming 'from all quarters' for the factory's goods, and nothing dates the first lodge, so the camp may be older than its range. It stood on the 14th, the scene date (Currey 1912 ch. III (lines 2239-2248), the view from the fort's walls on the evening of the last day, 14 August 1812: 'Toward the west was the Agency House, standing near the bank of the river, beyond which were the groups of Indian wigwams clustered along the creek that formerly flowed into the main stream at the present State Street.'), and on the 15th (Wau-Bun ch. XIX, Mrs. Helm's narrative of 15 August: led 'back towards the Chicago River, along the southern bank of which was the Pottowattamie encampment', to 'one of the wigwams', where water was dipped 'from a stream that flowed near' (Kinzie's footnote 36: 'Along the present State Street').). It closes on 16 August, the morning the fort was burned (Wau-Bun ch. XIX); when the gathering broke up after that no source read here says, and the 16th is the bound this project chose. Nothing of 1835 can draw it. Other work; the groups rebuilt by other work.

levels.8-10: This is the camp of the gathering in August 1812. Two events date it, not the day it was set up. It starts on 12 August 1812. Wau-Bun says the Native people came from nearby villages, and a meeting was held with them that afternoon. So they were camped by then. Heald's letter says they came from all sides for the trading house's goods. No paper dates the first lodge, so the camp may be older. It stood on the 14th. Currey describes the view from the fort's walls that evening: the Agent's house by the river, and beyond it groups of Native lodges along the creek where State Street is now. It stood on the 15th too. Wau-Bun says Mrs. Helm was led back toward the river, to the camp on its south bank, and into one of the lodges by a stream. It ends on 16 August, the morning the fort was burned. No paper says when the people left after that. The 16th is our choice. It is not in the 1835 town.

entries.card: why:THE CAMP'S PLACE IS THE SOURCES', THIS GROUND IS OURS. Currey puts the gathering's lodges 'clustered along the creek' at the later State Street on 14 August (1912 ch. III) and Wau-Bun the encampment on the river's south bank with a stream beside it (ch. XIX); other work's six grounds stand there. Helm's count of 679 people needs more roofs than those six give, so this ground is added to the cluster. On the flat between the mouth group and the horse ground: local E +696..+732, N -100..-72. Chosen by a search on the committed the 1830 natural ground heightfield (the research notes on gathering camp 1812): its outline lies between -0.02 and +0.00 m of the origin's 0.80 m, every point 6 m outside it stands above 0.6 m (off the creek's cut), and it keeps 10 m from the other camp grounds, 15 m from every other 1812 footprint, 6 m from every worn trail and 4 m from the 1835 inferred households' footprints. The point recorded is the ground's south-west corner, the footprint's origin at rotation 0. “Lodges for the whole August 1812 gathering: seven more grounds on the creek, the occupancy rule, and a camp for Wells's Miami escort”. THE PLATTED STREET IS REFUSED IN WRITING: the ground laps the corridor of Dearborn Street, which Thompson's plat of 4 August 1830 (Thompson, James. Plat of the Town of Chicago) laid out eighteen years after this camp's one phase, so the camp and the street never stand in one scene; the corridor intrusion baseline tool carries the refusal, as it does other work's horse ground and the first fort's cornfield and wharf.

levels.8-10: There are windows and doors in both ends of the house. On the west end, Sarony draws a small window high under the roof, a window near the back of the wall, and a door near the front with a step. We read their places from his picture. Two other pictures draw the same small window high up. Two more draw something dark high up and a pale mark low on the wall, where Sarony puts his window and door. On the east end, Eastman, in the oldest picture from 1820, draws two small windows side by side, high on the wall. We put them in the log wall, just under the roof. Window and door widths are like the ones on the front. The west door is 2.5 meters tall. None of these sizes was measured long ago.

entries.card: why:THE FAR END HIPPED, AS EASTMAN DRAWS IT (owner's ruling 2026-10-22). One small figure in one engraving is the whole of the evidence.

entries.card: why:THE KINZIE YEARS, AS THE HOUSE'S OWN RANGE, AND BOTH ENDS INFERRED FOR THIS BUILDING. No source dates this building. Wau-Bun ch. XVII names the establishment's buildings as Juliette Kinzie found them in 1831 (dairy, bake-house, lodging-house for the Frenchmen, stables), and Eastman's 1820 view and the three pictures of about 1831-1833 draw draws this one; neither is a sighting of 1812. It is taken to stand from the Kinzies' purchase in the fall of 1804 (The Kinzie house, built by Jean Baptiste Point du Sable's opening, Currey ch. II) through the 1812 scene dates (1 and 14 August) to the end of 1833 with the house it served: Currey says the house 'escaped the general destruction at the time of the massacre', nothing read says the yard behind it burned, and the family was away from 1812 to 1816, so the 1820 and 1831 pictures show a yard that was either standing in 1812 or rebuilt on its ground after the return; this record takes the first. It closes with the house (the exclusions record John Kinzie House (the old Kinzie mansion): derelict from 1832, gone by 1835), so it stands in no 1835 view. “The Kinzie establishment of 1812: which pictured building is which, where the unpictured ones stand, their sizes, and the rulings on du Sable's bill of sale”.

entries.card: why:THE MAIN ROOF CARRIED DOWN OVER THE PIAZZA AT A BREAK. Lossing, the Cram plate and the Teich painting draw one plane from the ridge to the piazza's eave; the 1857 engraving draws a flatter roof below the main one. Sarony's lithograph of Juliette Kinzie's sketch, the one picture by a member of the household, and Eastman's 1820 engraving, the earliest, both draw the two together: the front slope breaks to a flatter pitch over the piazza, so seen from afar it is one plane run down to the posts and seen close it is a break. Built as that: a flatter plane rising from the piazza's plate until it meets the main slope above the front wall (the log dwelling generator _swept piazza roof). Other work had built the 1857 reading, a separate roof hung under the main eave.

entries.card: why:THE OPENING IS A DATED MENTION AND THE CLOSE IS A BOUND THIS PROJECT CHOSE. It opens on 6 April 1812, the evening Captain Heald's letter of 15 April puts a party at 'Messrs. Russell and Lee's cabin, in a field on the Portage branch of the Chicago river' (Moses and Kirkland 1895, p. 43, the moses kirkland history of chicago v1 data lines 6878-6885): the first dated day a source puts the cabin on the ground. It is older than that, and no source says how much: Currey has it 'built some time after Fort Dearborn had been established' (the plate's caption, Gutenberg #52346 plain text lines 1482-1487), so after 1803. It closes at the end of 1822, the last year a source puts a house on the same premises: Gurdon Hubbard, as Hurlbut printed him (the hurlbut chicago antiquities 28 36 data lines 58-61), sets John Crafts's trading house 'about half a mile below Bridgeport, ("Hardscrabble" - the same premises, where in April 1812, two murders were committed by the Indians)', and 'In 1822, Crafts succumbed, and engaged himself to the American Fur Company' (same, lines 61-64). Whether Crafts traded from Lee's cabin or built his own is not known, so the close is a bound and not a reading (“Lee's Place in 1812: the cabin's seat, size and shape, the field's bounds and fence, and the closing date”). It is out of 1835 either way.

entries.card: why:THE OPENING IS A DATED MENTION AND THE CLOSE IS A BOUND THIS PROJECT CHOSE. It opens on 7 April 1812, the day Lee's son ran down from Lee's Place to give the alarm (Wau-Bun ch. XIX: the family 'had resided in a house on the Lake shore, not far from the fort'); that is the first dated day a source ties to the household, and the house may well be older, since Lee was cultivating his South Branch farm before it. It was standing on 18 August 1812: Currey lists 'that lately occupied by Charles Lee and his family near the mouth of the river' among the four houses left after the burning (ch. III). Moses and Kirkland say 'the house built by Charles Lee south of the fort was sold in 1812 to' Jean Baptiste Beaubien (the moses kirkland history of chicago v1 data lines 9785-9789) and say nothing of it after. No source read for other work says when it came down. It is closed at the end of 1817, the year Moses and Kirkland's same paragraph ends its account of the post-war houses (Jouett in the Burns house, Crafts at Lee's farm, both 1817): it stands through what that paragraph describes and in no scene this project draws after it, so it is out of 1835. The close is reconstructed (“The Burns and Lee houses of 1812: their seats, sizes, fabric and closing dates”); a dated record of the house after 1817 replaces it.

entries.card: why:THE PLACE IS CURREY'S, THIS GROUND IS OURS. Currey puts the Potawatomi's favourite camping place 'on the south bank near the present State Street bridge', where the creek opened into the river (ch. II, Gutenberg #52346 plain text lines 1360-1369). The creek's mouth itself is the August gathering's landing group (The Potawatomi camp of August 1812: the lodges by the creek's mouth), so this ground stands on the same bank a little west of it, between the river and the north-flat group: local E +698..+724, N -34..-16. Chosen by a search on the committed the 1830 natural ground heightfield (the research notes on trading lodges 1812): its outline lies between -0.02 and +0.00 m of the origin's 0.77 m, every point 6 m outside it stands above 0.6 m (off the cut of the river and the creek), and it keeps 10 m from the camp grounds, 15 m from every other 1812 footprint, 6 m from every worn trail and 4 m from the 1835 inferred households' footprints. The point recorded is the ground's south-west corner, the footprint's origin at rotation 0. “Potawatomi lodges by the river all 1812: a small camp on the south bank a little west of the creek's mouth, drawn every day”. THE PLATTED STREET IS REFUSED IN WRITING: the ground laps the corridor of Dearborn Street, which Thompson's plat of 4 August 1830 (Thompson, James. Plat of the Town of Chicago) laid out eighteen years after this camp's one phase, so the camp and the street never stand in one scene; the corridor intrusion baseline tool carries the refusal, as it does other work's north-flat ground and other work's horse ground.

entries.card: why:THE PLACE IS QUAIFE'S WORDS AND THE SHEET'S ARRANGEMENT; THE OUTLINE IS A RULING. Quaife, reading Whistler's description: 'Close to the forks on the south side of the main river a small field of eight or nine acres had been reduced to cultivation and made to serve as the company gardens and public cornfield.' The draught draws it the same way: a dotted outline lettered 'Company Garden & public Cornfield Eight acres' on the fort's side of the river where the branch comes in, with the 'Medow Ground sufficient for the Garrison' and the timber south of it. On the committed forks water (Wright 1834, +/-20 m) the field is laid square to the grid south of the main stem, its north fence about 26 m back from the south bank at its west end and more to the east, and its west fence about 90 m east of the South Branch, so that neither bank's uncertainty can put a rail in the river. WHAT FIXES ITS EDGES IS NOT EVIDENCE: the sheet's dotted outline is drawn 'without any Regular rule', so the record's rectangle was drawn to stand clear of what this project's own gate keeps every footprint of any date off, the 1835 inferred households' roofs (the inferred households generator holds every record three metres from them): Temple's Lake Street building fixes its east fence, the cooperage on South Water Street its north fence, the sawpit shed its west fence and the two sawyers' houses its south fence, all twenty-three years later and nothing to do with 1808. THE STREETS IT LIES ACROSS ARE THE 1830 PLAT'S, and it is refused in writing for them (the corridor intrusion baseline tool): the field closed with the first fort on 16 August 1812, eighteen years before Thompson's plat laid out a street here, so no street corridor and this fence ever stand in one scene; a field of the sheet's eight acres by the forks cannot be laid in this ground without crossing the later plat's streets, and moving it off them would move it away from the forks Quaife puts it beside (“The forks of 1812: the two houses Whistler draws there, Clark taken for one of them, and the company cornfield as a rail-fenced eight acres”).

levels.8-10: The place comes from Quaife's words and the old map. Its shape is our choice. Quaife says that near the fork of the river, on the south side, a small field of eight or nine acres was dug up for the soldiers' garden and the town's corn. The map draws it the same way, marked eight acres, on the fort's side of the river where the branch comes in. There is grass land and woods south of it. entries.card: why:THE PLACE IS THE SOURCES', THE SPOT IS OURS. Currey puts the Potawatomi's habitual camping place at the creek or swale that opened into the river at the later State Street bridge (Currey 1912 ch. II (Gutenberg #52346 plain text, lines 1360-1365): 'their favorite camping place being at a point on the south bank near the present State Street bridge. A swale or gully opened into the river there, reaching back as far as the present line of Randolph Street.'), and the gathering's lodges there on the scene date (ch. III, 'clustered along the creek'); Wau-Bun puts the encampment on the river's south bank with a stream beside it. The committed 1812 ground carries that creek as the state slough course and state slough mouth swales. So the camp is drawn on the creek's banks, never in its bed, in six grounds along its course (with the other potawatomi camp 1812_* records). Near the creek's head towards the later Randolph line: local E +616..+646, N -222..-198. This ground is the smallest group, furthest from the fort. Which bank, how far apart and where each rectangle sits are this project's, chosen on level ground: measured on the the 1830 natural ground heightfield its outline lies between -0.01 and +0.00 m of the origin's 0.85 m (the walker's tolerance is 0.35 m), and it stands 5.2 m from the swale's cut. Nothing else of 1812 stands on it; the 1835 town's footprints that later cover parts of it never stand on the same date. The point recorded is the ground's south-west corner, the footprint's origin at rotation 0. “The Potawatomi camp of August 1812: its six grounds on the creek, its lodges, arbors, hearths, gear and horse ground, and every form's shape and size”.

entries.card: why:THE RANGE IS BOUNDED BY THE DRAUGHT AND BY SILENCE, NOT BY A DATE FOR THIS HOUSE. It opens on 25 January 1808, the date in the parade of Whistler's draught, the first day a source draws the house; it may be older (Quaife has the north side's houses at four from 1803). It is taken to stand through the 1812 scene dates (1 and 14 August) by continuity: nothing read says it was pulled down, burned or left before the evacuation. It closes on 30 June 1816, the day before the second fort's records open (Fort Dearborn — soldiers' barracks, 1816-07-01): after the war no source read names this house again, and Mrs. Callis's list of the north side in 1816 (Andreas p. 89) names a Mr. Bridges' house 'between Kinzie's and the Burns house' that may be one of the three no. 31 houses and is not dated before 1816, so this record stops where its own record does. Out of 1835. “La Lime's and Le Mai's houses of 1812: which drawn house is whose, the north bank's frame, their sizes, heights and closing dates”.

entries.card: why:THE RANGE IS BOUNDED BY TWO DATED MENTIONS AND ONE LATER BUILDING, NOT BY A DATE FOR THIS HOUSE. It opens on 7 April 1812, the afternoon the alarm from Lee's Place was called across the river to Burns's and Ensign Ronan's party brought the mother and her day-old infant down to the fort by boat (Wau-Bun ch. XVIII; Moses and Kirkland p. 58, the moses kirkland history of chicago v1 data lines 8558-8562). That is the first day a source puts the house on the bank; it may be older, and nothing dates its building. It was still standing on 18 August 1812, when Currey lists it among the four houses left after the fort and the agency house burned (ch. III). Moses and Kirkland have it 'occupied in 1817 by Charles Jouett, the first United States Indian Agent' (lines 9797-9806), and the agency house afterwards called Cobweb Castle, 'commenced during Judge Jouett's incumbency' and completed by Wolcott about 1820, was put up 'near the spot' (Wau-Bun ch. XVIII n. 30; the record of Indian Agency House). So it closes at the end of 1819, the day before Indian Agency House opens: no source says whether the agency house was raised beside it, over it or out of it, and closing it then keeps the two from ever standing in one scene and keeps it out of 1835. the exclusions record carries no entry for it because no 1835 source was found that names it.

Currey lists it as one of four houses left after the fort and the agent's house burned. Moses and Kirkland say Charles Jouett, the first Native agent, lived in it in 1817. No paper says if the new house was built beside it, on it, or out of it. Ending it then keeps the two from standing at the same time, and keeps it out of the 1835 town.

entries.card: why:THE RANGE IS INFERRED FROM TWO WITNESSES OF 1808 AND A BOUND THIS PROJECT CHOSE. It opens on 25 January 1808, the date Whistler's draught carries, the one day a source shows the house standing; Surgeon Cooper, at the post from 1808, counts 'one near the forks of the river occupied by a man named Clark who was a cattle dealer' (Quaife 1913 p. 167). It may be older. No source read for other work mentions it after Cooper's years, so its standing on the scene date of August 1812 is inferred from continuity, as the La Lime house's is. It is closed on 3 July 1816, the day before the troops came back to rebuild the fort: nothing read names a house at the forks in any account of the reoccupied post, and the close keeps it out of every scene after 1812 rather than carrying an unwitnessed house into one. The close is reconstructed (“The forks of 1812: the two houses Whistler draws there, Clark taken for one of them, and the company cornfield as a rail-fenced eight acres”).

entries.card: why:THE RANGE IS THE FIRST FORT'S, NOT THIS COMPONENT'S. It opens on 17 August 1803, the day Swearingen's detachment reached the river at the bend where the fort was to be built (his journal, printed by Quaife), and closes on 16 August 1812, the day after the evacuation, when the fort was burned (the exclusions record The first Fort Dearborn (1803–1812)). No source dates any single building inside it: the fort was built over the months after the arrival, and Whistler's draught of 25 January 1808 is the one day on which every component here is shown standing. It ends before the second fort's 1816 phases begin, so no scene date can resolve the two forts together.

entries.card: why:THE RULING other work LEFT OPEN: whitewash or the wash drawing's shorthand. Built whitewashed, at the reconstructed grade. The plate draws the walls of the house smooth and pale with no courses and no notched corners, while it draws the lean-to's boards in strokes, the fence's rails one by one and the stack's shaded side dark: its maker drew texture where he saw it, so the pale wall is more likely a coat than a convention. Lime whitewash on a log house is the common frontier finish. No source here says the cabin was whitewashed, and a monochrome wash drawing a century later cannot prove it (“Lee's Place cabin built to the Currey plate: its openings' sizes, the stack's place on its gable, the lean-to and the whitewash”).

levels.8-10: Was the house painted white, or is that just how the picture was drawn? We built it painted white, and that is our guess. The picture draws the walls smooth and pale, with no rows of logs and no corners. But it draws the boards of the shed in lines, the fence rails one by one, and the chimney's dark side. The artist drew rough parts where he saw them. So the pale wall is more likely paint than just a way of drawing. Lime wash on a log house was common on the frontier. entries.card: why:THE TWO SOURCES DISAGREE IN WORDS AND NOT ON THIS GROUND. Wau-Bun ch. XIX puts the house 'on the Lake shore, not far from the fort'. Currey 1912 ch. II puts it 'near the fort on the bank of the river opposite where it discharged into the lake; which was near the present intersection of Madison Street and Michigan Avenue', and adds the reason: 'a long sand-bar prevented the river from finding an outlet directly in line with its course, and the current was forced to creep along close to the shore for some distance toward the south.' Ch. VIII says the same: 'On the bank of the river, near its mouth, stood the house of Charles Lee.' Moses and Kirkland have it 'south of the fort'. THE RULING: on this project's 1812 ground (the shoreline data) the river ran south behind the spit, and its west bank ends at the adopted outlet station, local E +1163.8, N -426.8, where the lake shore runs on south. At that one place the river bank and the lake shore are the same bank, so the house is seated there, west of the waterline, and both writers are right. Its east wall stands about 29 m west of the outlet station and about 22 m from the lake shore south of it; the ground there reads +2.4 m, the dry back of the beach. WHERE CURREY'S STREET NAMES AND THIS GROUND DIFFER: Madison Street is local N -519, 80 m south of the house. That gap is the spread between this ground's two readings of the mouth itself (the adopted Swearingen half-mile station and the 'madison street compilation' alternative, 94.9 m apart, shoreline.geojson's mouth outlet reading band). Currey wrote his intersection with the second reading in mind; this record keeps the house opposite the mouth the ground draws, because 'opposite where it discharged' is his claim and 'Madison Street' his gloss on where that was. If the ground's mouth moves, the house moves with it. Nothing dates its facing; rotation 0 is a reconstruction.

Currey puts it near the fort, on the bank of the river, across from where the river ran into the lake. He says that was near Madison Street and Michigan Avenue today. entries.card: why:THREE SOURCES PUT IT AT THE FOOT OF STATE STREET AND ONE PUTS IT CLOSER TO THE LAKE; THIS RECORD TAKES THE THREE. Wau-Bun, n. 30 to ch. XVIII: 'Burns's house stood near the spot where the Agency Building, or "Cobweb Castle," was afterwards erected, at the foot of N. State Street.' Moses and Kirkland, the moses kirkland history of chicago v1 data lines 9797-9802: 'near what is now the southwest corner of North State (formerly Wolcott) and Water streets'. Currey 1912 ch. II: the alarm was called 'to John Burns, then living in a cabin on the north bank of the river near' the later State Street bridge, and ch. III sets the house on the north bank opposite the creek that came in at State Street. THE ALTERNATIVE, STATED AND NOT TAKEN: Moses and Kirkland p. 36 (lines 5630-5640) give Hurlbut's judgment that the Burns house was the log house Wau-Bun puts 'on the north side of the river some two or three hundred yards from the lake and twenty steps from the river bank', at 'about the northeast corner of north State and North Water streets'. On this project's 1812 ground the lake is about 600 m east of State Street at this northing, so two or three hundred yards (183-274 m) from it would seat the house near local E +1000..+1100, on the north bank opposite the fort, where the histories put the Kinzie house instead. The two readings cannot both hold, and the street corner is the one three writers give. FROM HURLBUT THIS RECORD KEEPS ONE FIGURE, the twenty steps from the river bank, because it does not disagree with the corner: the south wall stands 15.2 m (twenty paces of 2.5 ft) north of the north bank of the shoreline data, which reads N +92.1 at this easting. SOUTHWEST OVER NORTHEAST: Moses and Kirkland write both corners, Hurlbut's 'northeast' on p. 36 and their own 'southwest' later. The southwest corner is the one between Water Street and the river, so it is the one that keeps the twenty steps; it is also the corner Wau-Bun gives for Cobweb Castle, which Wau-Bun puts 'near the spot'. THE EXACT SEAT IS THIS PROJECT'S: the house stands west of Indian Agency House's footprint (local E +801..+814, N +113..+122) and clear of it, so the later building does not stand on this one in plan. Nothing dates which way the house faced; rotation 0 is a reconstruction.

levels.8-10: Three books put this house at the foot of State Street, and one puts it closer to the lake. We go with the three. Wau-Bun says Burns's house stood near where the agent's house, Cobweb Castle, was built later, at the foot of North State Street. Moses and Kirkland say it was near the south-west corner of North State and Water Streets. Currey says Burns lived in a cabin on the north bank of the river near the State Street bridge, across from the creek. Hurlbut thought it was a log house two or three hundred yards from the lake and twenty steps from the river. On our ground, the lake is about 600 meters east of State Street. Two or three hundred yards from the lake would put it right where the Kinzie house is. Both cannot be true, and three writers give the street corner. From Hurlbut we keep one thing: twenty steps from the river. That fits the corner. So the south wall is about 15 meters north of the river bank. Moses and Kirkland name both corners, north-east and south-west. The south-west one is between Water Street and the river, so it keeps the twenty steps. The exact spot is our choice. It stands just west of the later agent's house, clear of it. Which way the house faced is our guess.

entries.card: why:The 1912 plate draws a zigzag rail fence along the bank and round the field: a worm (snake) fence. The plate is a modern reconstruction, so this is inferred from it and from the type, which is what a frontier farm without a post-hole digger built.

levels.8-10: A picture from 1912 draws a zigzag rail fence along the river and round the field. It is a snake fence. The picture was made long after, so this is our best guess from it. It is also the kind of fence a frontier farm built when it had no tool to dig post holes.

entries.card: why:The Burns family's house. THE SOURCES DISAGREE ON THE HUSBAND'S FIRST NAME, AND THE RECORD DOES NOT RULE: Moses and Kirkland think its occupant 'probable' to be 'the "Thomas Burns" who appears in the Fort Dearborn muster roll, 1810', enlisted 8 June 1806 and so due his discharge on 8 June 1811 (the moses kirkland history of chicago v1 data lines 8548-8556); Currey 1912 calls him John Burns throughout. Neither cites a document for the name it gives. Wau-Bun calls the house only 'Burns's'.

Moses and Kirkland think he was probably the Thomas Burns on the fort's list of soldiers in 1810. That man joined on 8 June 1806, so he was due to leave the army on 8 June 1811. entries.card: why:The United States factory: the government trading house that sold goods to the Potawatomi and other nations for furs, with the factor's quarters. Identified as this building by other work (register § outside the stockade, part 'factory'): it is the paled house due west of the fort, where the Chicago Magazine of 1857 puts 'the two-story log United States factory', and of Quaife's 'two log houses' a short distance to the south-west it is the one without the numeral 17.

levels.8-10: This was the government's trading house. It sold goods to the Potawatomi and other nations for furs. The trade agent lived in it too. We worked out that this is that building. It is the house with a fence, right west of the fort. The Chicago Magazine of 1857 puts the two-story log trading house there. Quaife names two log houses a short way to the south-west. This is the one without the number 17.

entries.card: why:The house's own range (The Kinzie house, built by Jean Baptiste Point du Sable). THE KINZIE YEARS, BOTH ENDS INFERRED. It opens in the fall of 1804, when Currey has John Kinzie buy the house from Le Mai and arrive 'in the fall of that year' (Currey, J. Seymour. The Story of Old Fort Dearborn, ch. II); Moses and Kirkland give Le Mai 1796 where Currey gives 1797, and the Kinzies' arrival is put at 1803 elsewhere, so the opening is the later of the two readings and the house stands earlier than this phase says, under du Sable and Le Mai, in a form no picture shows. It covers 1 and 14 August 1812: Currey, 'The house escaped the general destruction at the time of the massacre'. It closes at the end of 1833: Currey says it 'was finally demolished in the early thirties', the 1857 engraving shows it about 1833, and the exclusions record John Kinzie House (the old Kinzie mansion) rules it unoccupied and 'dilapidated beyond repair' from 1832 and gone by 1835, so it stands in no 1835 view.

levels.8-10: These are the house's dates. It starts in the fall of 1804. Currey says John Kinzie bought the house from Le Mai that year and came that fall. Other books give other years, so we chose the later one. The house is older than that. Du Sable and Le Mai lived in it before, in a shape no picture shows. It stood in August 1812. It was empty and falling down from 1832 and gone by 1835. So it is not in the 1835 town.

entries.card: why:WHICH HOUSE IS WHOSE IS THIS PROJECT'S, AND IT IS GRADED SO. Cooper, post surgeon from 1808, counted four houses on the north side in his time, 'occupied by Kinzie, Ouilmette, La Lime, and Le Mai' (Quaife 1913 p. 166); Whistler's draught of January 1808 draws Kinzie's and three more west of it, and names none. Quaife pairs the two. The assignment: Ouilmette takes the no. 31 house nearest Kinzie's, because Currey has his cabin 'close in the rear of the Kinzie house' and Wau-Bun 'close at hand' (builds it); the other two take Cooper's remaining names in the order he gives them, walking west, La Lime the middle house and Le Mai the westernmost. Cooper's order is not stated to be an order on the ground. “La Lime's and Le Mai's houses of 1812: which drawn house is whose, the north bank's frame, their sizes, heights and closing dates”.

levels.8-10: Which house belonged to whom is our guess. Cooper, the fort's doctor from 1808, counted four houses on the north side. He says Kinzie, Ouilmette, La Lime and Le Mai lived in them. Whistler's map of January 1808 draws Kinzie's house and three more west of it, but names none. Quaife puts the two together. We gave Ouilmette the house nearest Kinzie's. Currey says his cabin was close behind the Kinzie house, and Wau-Bun says close at hand. The other two take Cooper's other names in his order, going west. La Lime gets the middle house and Le Mai the far west one. Cooper does not say his order is the order on the ground.

entries.card: why:WHO LIVED IN OUILMETTE'S HOUSE IS THE SOURCES'; WHICH DRAWN HOUSE WAS HIS IS INFERRED. Currey (1912, ch. II): 'Ouilmette was a Frenchman with an Indian wife, and had lived here since 1790. His wife, being a member of the Potawatami tribe, was awarded... a tract of land on the north shore', the Wilmette Reservation; and in the August chapter, 'A sister of his wife, known in the accounts as Mrs. Bisson, was a member of this same household.' Wau-Bun ch. XIX describes both women as of mixed descent. Victoire Porthier, born Mirandeau, remembered that 'some of us lived in the Ouilmette house across the river from the fort' before the fort burned (Moses and Kirkland v1, lines 6776-6779 of the committed text). The house is the no. 31 house nearest Kinzie's because Currey puts Ouilmette's cabin 'close in the rear of the Kinzie house' and Wau-Bun 'close at hand' ('s assignment, “La Lime's and Le Mai's houses of 1812: which drawn house is whose, the north bank's frame, their sizes, heights and closing dates”).

levels.8-10: Old books say who lived in Ouilmette's house. Which house on the map was his is our guess. Currey says Ouilmette was a Frenchman. His wife was Native, a Potawatomi. He had lived here since 1790. She was given land on the north shore, where Wilmette is now. Currey also says her sister, Mrs. Bisson, lived with them. Wau-Bun says both women had Native and French parents. Victoire Porthier said some of her family lived in the Ouilmette house, across the river from the fort, before it burned. entries.card: why:Wau-Bun: the garden 'extended to the north of the dwelling'. Whistler's draught of 1808 draws the Kinzie house in a fenced yard lettered as Mr Kinzie's kitchen garden (the register's no. 30, read at), with the old horse mill outside it to the west. So the garden lies north of the house and its yard of outbuildings, its west side east of the mill. Its corners are this record's (the liberties register “The Kinzie establishment of 1812: which pictured building is which, where the unpictured ones stand, their sizes, and the rulings on du Sable's bill of sale”).

entries.card: why:Whistler's draught of 25 January 1808 draws two small houses at the bottom left of the sheet, where the double line of the river (index no. 25) meets a second double line lettered 'One branch of Cheykago River': one in the angle between the branch and the river, across the river from the fort, and one on the fort's side of the river beside the dotted outline lettered 'Company Garden & public Cornfield Eight acres'. Quaife (1913 p. 167): 'Whistler's drawing represents two houses at the forks, one occupied by a discharged soldier.' The committed trace's 34-item index does not number them; they were found on the pinned sheet at other work. THE RULING: the draught's 'One branch' is the North Branch, because the river line it meets is the main stem coming round from the fort and the cornfield Quaife puts 'on the south side of the main river' is drawn on the fort's side of that line; so this house, drawn across the main stem from the fort and on the near side of the branch, stands on the north bank east of the North Branch. On the committed forks water (Wright 1834, +/-20 m) it is seated about 75 m east of the North Branch's east bank and 50 m north of the main stem's north bank, far enough that the bank's own uncertainty cannot put it in the water. The sheet's distances here are not to any scale, so nothing nearer is claimed. Rotation 0 is a reconstruction (“The forks of 1812: the two houses Whistler draws there, Clark taken for one of them, and the company cornfield as a rail-fenced eight acres”).
